title: The Press Is Not the Root of Trump’s Problems
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
President Trump is going through a rough patch—in foreign relations, in the economy, in the courts, and in election outlook—and he believes that he has found the culprits: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico
On Friday, Trump said he was banning the three outlets from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS” and warned that more bans could come
When he feels beleaguered, he tends to lash out at familiar enemies, especially reporters
The idea that negative coverage is to blame for his predicament is perversely flattering
But Trump’s true scourge is reality, not how the news is covering it
Although the decision is part of a gradually intensifying attack on free speech, as I noted last month , it has drawn particular pushback

This morning, five major TV networks (including Fox News) agreed to suspend pool coverage of the president and White House events after CNN was blocked from its previously assigned spot in a pool rotation today
The three banned outlets also sued over their exclusion

How such a suit will fare is unclear; Trump banned the Associated Press from the White House press pool last year after it refused to adopt his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico, and a lawsuit challenging the ban is still pending

After Trump committed a Kinsley gaffe on Friday by calling his move “the ban on the free press,” he tried to clean up his spin this morning. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish
It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,” he wrote , claiming that it “is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” This is nonsense
Trump has every right to hate the way he’s covered, but if the government has the power to decide what is fake and what is true, then the press is not free
Trump’s post demonstrates his talismanic belief in the power of news coverage

The president himself has been obsessed with attention—how to get it and how to shape it—for his entire life, and he is a relic from an era when the media were so dominant, and had such control over the means of reaching an audience, that they seemed to shape reality

They are much diminished today, occupying a strange, unstable role: strong enough to be blamed for both Trump’s rise and his downfall, yet weak enough that they can be threatened with relative impunity
Though Trump’s attacks on free speech are unlike any in living memory, his is not the first administration to believe that its problems are about messaging and coverage

In 2012, Barack Obama said that the biggest mistake of his first term “was thinking that this job was just about getting the policy right,” because “the nature of this office is also to tell a story to the American people.” A decade later, Joe Biden’s administration was convinced that negative coverage of inflation and Biden’s age were bigger problems than inflation or the president’s evident frailty

He is not unpopular because of Politico , an outlet that focuses largely on Washington machinations, or because of MS NOW or CNN, two cable channels that—as he is fond of pointing out —have relatively small audiences for television
The media cannot be “failing” and all-powerful at the same time

Trump is unpopular because (to name a few big reasons) he is losing a war of choice to Iran, making inflation worse without seeming to care how voters feel, overreaching with draconian immigration enforcement, and focusing on vanity projects that don’t matter to voters

Ironically, Trump is committing the same error as many liberal critics of the press, who seem to believe that popular support for the president would have collapsed long ago if the media had used harsher words to describe him
But the idea that tougher coverage would have stopped him is fantasy

Although the press has made many mistakes in how it has reported on the president, including giving him hours of uninterrupted TV air time in 2016, downplaying bigoted remarks , and “ sanewashing ” some statements, Trump has also received more intensive investigation and negative coverage than any president in American history
Some of that coverage has surely been hackish partisanship—which is protected by the First Amendment too—but much of it has been earned
Newspapers, magazines, wire services, and TV networks have turned out a series of scoops about the chaos inside the administration, Trump’s policy errors, and the pervasive corruption around him
In late 2023, The Atlantic published a series of prescient essays considering what would happen if Trump won back the White House
Voters had even lived through one Trump presidency already
They had access to the relevant information before they voted him in again

Believing that Americans might have chosen differently if only The New York Times had abandoned its obtuse headline conventions is comforting to some Trump critics, because it puts the blame on the press rather than acknowledging that a majority of those who voted wanted Trump
By the same token, Trump would rather blame news outlets he does not like than confront the reality that some of those same voters are rejecting him because of his choices
The president faces an additional risk in trying to ban these three outlets
He detests adversarial coverage, but he desperately desires attention
This afternoon, Trump spoke with reporters outside the White House
Usually, his comments are captured by the boom mics from the pool TV team, but without their presence today, he was inaudible
Censorship can silence anyone, it turns out—even the censor
Related: Trump’s attacks on the media are self-defeating
The pinball president Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : The Pangram backlash unfolding on college campuses Don’t ask how this war ends, Eliot A
The northern passage Tom Nichols on Trump’s monumental obsession Today’s News Protesters gathered in Austin after an immigration enforcement officer shot and injured a man in the city yesterday

title: The Confrontation That Broke New York
excerpt: In the spring of 2023, a young Black man stepped onto a subway car in Manhattan
body: In the spring of 2023, a young Black man stepped onto a subway car in Manhattan
He screamed, threw garbage at passengers, and announced that he was prepared to die
New Yorkers often encase themselves in psychological armor on the subway, but for many of the riders in that car, this was too much
A woman hid her face in a friend’s chest; a mother tried to hide behind her stroller with her toddler
Then a 24-year-old white man, an ex-Marine, grabbed the screaming man and put him in a neck lock, and five minutes later—by mistake? Intentionally?—left that man dead on the floor of the subway car

To read the new book on that killing, Man in the Mirror: Hope, Struggle, and Belonging in an American City , by Anand Giridharadas, is to recognize that the membrane separating safety and fear on the New York City subways appeared in danger of rupturing by 2023
In the preceding few years, dozens of people had been pushed onto subway tracks, suffering injury or death
The tension between chaos and order—often evident in New York—could be acute
Before anyone could sort out the facts, too many people rushed to impose narratives
Jordan Neely became the homeless Black man with the too-disposable life; Daniel Penny became the muscular vigilante who grew up in the white-bread suburbs

Leftist activists howled racism; right-wing sorts adjusted their ties and talked tough. “In a civilized society, the strong protect the weak,” a member of The Wall Street Journal ’s editorial board wrote. “A Marine uses his strength to fight for those unable to fight for themselves.” Liberal politicians divined morality tales

Brad Lander, at the time the city comptroller, who lives in a prosperous liberal precinct in Brooklyn, proclaimed: “We must not become a city where a mentally ill human being can be choked to death by a vigilante without consequence.” I wanted to say: Stop, please
Try not to talk of consequences and militarization and the menace of the streets until we have a clue about how to prevent this from happening again
There is pathos enough to be found in basic facts

In his book, Giridharadas takes on the considerable challenge of telling a story that encompasses conflicting narratives and the voices of nearly every player: defense attorneys, people living on the street, public-health officials, both Neely and Penny
His writing is most powerful when he traces the threads of tragically entwined lives
Whereas some in the media reduced Neely to a trope—the mentally ill homeless man— Man in the Mirror invests his life with complication and nuance
His mother was killed by her boyfriend; in a gothic twist, that boyfriend cross-examined young Jordan while representing himself at his trial
In time, Neely drifted further and further away from those who wanted to offer him succor

The reader learns about outreach workers and prosecutors who were ambivalent on how to treat his illness, and about well-meaning bureaucrats whose actions fell short. [ Read: The heart of the debate over Jordan Neely’s death ] Here and there, the author stumbles when inserting liberal punctuation points

He argues that addressing crime is an inescapable fact of life for Democrats, even if the fear that crime is out of control is “based in nonreality.” The biggest problem, he writes, is a nation “awash in anxiety and fear: of change, of the social advancement of marginalized populations, of losing control of children, of losing control of the border, of losing cultural status and centrality, of the Other, of chaos.” This strikes me as too easy
Change, demographic and otherwise, has swept through and revitalized New York City for centuries
And the subways are arteries that give life to us all
I grew up riding the rails to see girlfriends and basketball games
My schoolmates and I rode to a Bronx public high school in train cars so encased in graffiti, we had to peer out of the opening doors to see if we’d reached our stop
Slowly, however, that system grew cleaner and safer
When the coronavirus pandemic overtook New York City, that momentum seemed to reverse, and the subways began to feel menacing again
My claim here is reality-based, drawing on statistics and personal experience
Assaults on the subway increased by 65 percent from 2020 to 2025, and the number of murders in the system spiked as well
And a year after Neely died, a man shoved a friend of my family onto the subway tracks
He suffered multiple fractures, and his rehabilitation stretched across brutal months
One morning in the spring of 2023, I was riding the Q train to the Upper East Side when I heard a booming voice and saw a great block of a man enter the subway car and ask for money
As the man approached, the timbre of his voice grew agitated
When the train stopped in the middle of a tunnel, the panhandler stood over a young man who sat across from me
He put out a massive hand. “You’re giving me money,” he announced

Silence followed as the young passenger kept eyes downcast. “Mutherfucker, I’ve got a big-ass knife”—the man patted his shaggy overcoat—“and I’m going to gut you from your balls to your throat.” I made eye contact with other men on the train
What the hell do we do if he pulls out that knife? If we are lucky enough to pull him to the floor, how do we keep him there? I offer none of this to sound macho
I’m a 60-something man with a strong desire to remain alive
I harbored no illusions about my ability to wrestle this man to the ground
As it happened, the train started and pulled into the next station and he got off, but not before loudly vowing to gut us all

title: What Were My Dreams Trying to Tell Me?
excerpt: Illustrations by Hélène Blanc W hen I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me
body: Illustrations by Hélène Blanc W hen I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me
The feeling was utterly concrete, though the result of no medical condition that any of the various doctors I saw could identify
The hole felt like a viscous emptiness—a paradox, admittedly, as any real emptiness should have felt like nothing
This was a nothing, but its nothingness very much felt like something—and something that was growing
Accompanying this feeling of an expanding hole at the center of me was a sense that I was losing more and more of myself to it, like shoreline eroded by rising waters
To lose myself felt less like oblivion than instability

I observed in myself a new susceptibility to the opinions of others, and a new recklessness, as if some dark, decisive action might either quiet my doubts about my fundamental worth or end my longing once and for all

I recall one particularly dangerous, drunken night that had me well over the legal limit, both aware that I was getting into a car that could kill me and others, and also not believing that any of it mattered
The onset of my devolving well-being was strange and sudden, and seemed connected to childhood in some way I couldn’t understand
I hadn’t been a tortured child but rather placid, if introverted
My parents always said that I had been easy to keep happy
It sometimes seemed to me as if the hole I was experiencing was one where some piece of my childhood had once resided
I was missing class in college, showing up to theater rehearsals drunk
A caring young woman I was dating could take no more of my savage, ranting mood swings and persistent despair
She broke up with me over tea at the student union and implored me to seek help
Even sleep was now fraught with violent, terrifying dreams—of rocket ships out of control, conflagrations and invasions, and, yes, holes into which I would disappear
But exactly what sort of help I might need, I didn’t know
I confided my woes to a friend who’d grown up on a farm in Kentucky
He never missed Sunday Mass, and when I told him about the hole inside me, he pulled a copy of The Seven Storey Mountain from his bag and handed it to me
Thomas Merton, he said, had written about something similar
It was what had led him to leave the world and become a monk
I found deep resonance in the book’s harrowing account of Merton’s time at Cambridge and Columbia—the intense restlessness and emptiness, the disgust and torpor and despair
But Merton’s solution was theistic: a turn to God that I could only read as naive and distorting
Even the passages that approached the specificity of my own experience were charged with personification that read as anachronistic at best: The room was very quiet
And as I lay in bed, in my weariness and pain and disgust, I felt for a moment the shadow of another visitor pass into the room
It was death, that came to stand by my bed
I kept my eyes closed, more out of apathy than anything else
But anyway, there was no need to open one’s eyes to see the visitor, to see death
Death is someone you see very clearly with eyes in the center of your heart: eyes that see not by reacting to light, but by reacting to a kind of a chill from within the marrow of your own life
I knew this experience: a central chill, a lightlessness connected to the doomed feeling of some ultimate end
But I resisted any characterization that departed from the fundamental sensation itself—of a growing hole inside me
For no reason I knew, I was convinced that remaining honest with myself about this basic fact was the only thing I could do to help myself
They flew out to visit me at school and figure out what was wrong
Over a meal they prepared for me in a hotel room with a kitchen, I confided in them
There was a hole inside me that I needed to address, I said
My mother found me a psychiatrist, an avuncular Brit who was more interested in my sex life than my interior void, which I insisted was more real than he seemed willing to allow
But something important endured from the handful of sessions I had with him
A volume on the shelf over his left ear drew my fascination, and would soon fill weeks of my life: Freud’s The Interpretation of Dreams
That book began a process in me, what I’ve often called “curiosity” when I’ve told this story, but which is probably better described as a form of relationship
The nightly tumult of disturbing dreams persisted, and even if I couldn’t be sure whether Freud was right about how to make sense of them, simply attempting to do so seemed to help

title: In Defense of Guilt by Association
excerpt: Vance and Abdul El-Sayed have very little in common ideologically and seem to like each other even less
body: Vance and Abdul El-Sayed have very little in common ideologically and seem to like each other even less

As part of a nasty exchange of personal insults last month, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan implied that Vance’s grandfather would disapprove of the vice president’s Indian American wife

In response , Vance called El-Sayed “very, very evil” and warned him to “keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth because she’s way out of your league.” Yet even as Vance and El-Sayed are happy to trade schoolyard taunts, they can agree on at least one thing: that guilt by association is a contemptible means of scoring cheap political points. “I’m tired of this guilt-by-association thing,” El-Sayed complained earlier this year, when he was asked about his decision to campaign alongside Hasan Piker, an internet shock jock who has said that “America deserved 9/11,” described allegations of sexual violence on October 7 as “rape fantasies,” and praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of the world,” among many other charming bon mots
Despite repeated calls from within his own party to renounce Piker, El-Sayed refuses to do so
Vance is facing a similar situation with his friend Tucker Carlson
Vance “ doesn’t believe in guilt-by-association cancel culture ,” a spokesperson said in September 2024, after the then-senator appeared onstage with the conservative podcast host

In the years since his firing from Fox News, Carlson has lauded a Holocaust denier as “the most important historian in the United States,” accused a small Jewish sect of orchestrating the war in Iran, and praised Vladimir Putin as “the most effective leader in my lifetime.” Carlson, whose show returns again and again to the supposed perfidy of the Jews, has become the country’s highest-profile promoter of anti-Semitism

He recently held a friendly conversation with a guest who claimed that algebra was “fake math” created for “goy slaves.” Vance was asked directly about his relationship with Carlson at a White House press conference earlier this month. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them
I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go.” [ Jonathan Chait: J

Vance’s disingenuous defense of Tucker Carlson ] El-Sayed and Vance would have us believe that their troublesome friends are no different from the people in our own lives whose political views we abhor but whom we nonetheless love and appreciate. “If I had to choose between betraying my country and betraying my friend, I hope I should have the guts to betray my country,” the English writer E
Forster wrote in 1938 as Europe hurtled toward war
It’s a noble sentiment, a paean to friendship over tribe
But Piker and Carlson are not the equivalent of your crazy uncle
And El-Sayed and Vance are not regular citizens; they’re political figures whose judgment and choices affect other Americans’ lives
One’s choice of friends is in fact an excellent sign of character, and in this respect, both Vance and El-Sayed have demonstrated a conspicuous lack of it

The tactic known as “guilt by association” evokes the legacy of Senator Joe McCarthy, whose feral zeal for exposing Communists, real or imagined, was so era-defining that it inspired the attachment of an ism to his surname
McCarthy’s sin wasn’t his anti-communism, however—there were indeed highly placed Soviet agents in the federal government
It was his recklessness and lack of concern for the truth
There has to be a reasonable middle ground between conducting a witch hunt and blatantly ignoring someone’s willingness to fraternize with genuinely disreputable people
Now that their associations are in the spotlight, El-Sayed, Vance, and their respective ideological compatriots are eager to minimize them

In a softball interview with Piker several months ago, the Pod Save Americ a host Jon Favreau, a prominent liberal opinion-shaper, said that he wants Democrats to take the “Don’t Talk About Hasan Piker For A Day Challenge.” Asked about Piker’s remarks concerning 9/11, El-Sayed tried to depict himself as a victim of the “cancel culture that all of us agreed was a bad idea back in 2020, but we seem to want to bring back.” A “Vance ally” echoed a similar sentiment to The Washington Post about the vice president’s relationship with Carlson, saying , “We’re done with the canceling, period.” No one should accept these evasions
In April, El-Sayed deployed Piker to boost support among young voters at Michigan State and the University of Michigan
In the final hours before polls closed, El-Sayed appeared at a pool party with Piker and other internet influencers in Detroit
Vance’s association with Carlson goes much deeper

In a 2021 interview recalling the time they first met, Vance described their immediate recognition of each other as “the guy who’s exactly right about what’s going on in the country.” Carlson helped persuade Donald Trump to select Vance as his running mate; Vance hired Carlson’s son as his deputy press secretary

When Vance guest-hosted Charlie Kirk’s show after the conservative activist’s assassination, one of the first people he invited into the vice-presidential suite was Carlson. (At Kirk’s funeral six days later, Carlson delivered a eulogy that seemed to imply that the Jews had murdered Kirk just as they had Jesus Christ.) The most obvious reason El-Sayed and Vance haven’t disowned their noxious friends is that both Piker and Carlson command large audiences
Politics is about winning votes, and a moral miscreant’s is worth the same as a saint’s
Other politicians have done much worse than associate with the likes of Piker and Carlson
What’s more troubling is that El-Sayed and Vance both appear to sympathize with at least some of what their influencer friend espouses
On multiple occasions, Vance has shown that he either doesn’t understand or doesn’t care about anti-Semitism

He once dismissed outrage over a group of Young Republicans joking about gas chambers as “pearl clutching” and characterized attempts to sideline bigots from the conservative movement as “endless, self-defeating purity tests.” One might think that Carlson’s frequent attacks on Vance’s boss, up to and including that Trump “ should be removed from office immediately ,” would have persuaded Vance, purely out of his own self-interest, to disavow Carlson
That he hasn’t done so indicates the high value he places on his association with him
If not for such data points, Vance’s friendship with Carlson would be easy to dismiss as misplaced affection for someone who helped advance his career
But Vance is on the record stating otherwise

Late last year, he said, I find the idea that Tucker Carlson—who has one of the largest podcasts in the world, who has millions of listeners, who supported Donald Trump in the 2024 election, who supported me in the 2024 election—the idea that his views are somehow completely anathema to conservatism, that he has no place in the conservative movement, is frankly absurd
This implies that Holocaust denial, claims of Jewish disloyalty to the United States, veneration of Putin, and a host of other poisonous ideas are welcome in the conservative movement

Even the white-nationalist influencer Nick Fuentes is fed up with Vance’s disingenuousness. “JD Vance panders to the far right but simply doesn’t want the baggage of associating with the far right,” Fuentes told The New York Times . “If he has a problem with ‘antisemites,’ then he should start by disavowing his best friend Tucker Carlson.” [ Read: The Hasan Piker question ] A similar ideological affinity appears to exist between Piker and El-Sayed, whose past statements on 9/11 and terrorism more broadly have a way of creating a moral equivalency between the United States and its Islamist enemies. “Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my faith,” El-Sayed tweeted five years ago on the 20th anniversary of the attacks. “Tomorrow, I’ll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my country.” Earlier this year, after a Hezbollah-inspired terrorist rammed his car into a Detroit-area synagogue where 140 preschool-age Jewish children were playing, El-Sayed said that “hurt people hurt people,” a reference to the fact that the attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli air strike. (In a clumsy attempt at an apology, El-Sayed stubbornly refused to acknowledge the odious logic of his remarks, allowing only that he had chosen to administer “the right medicine at the wrong time.”) Like Prince Hal banishing Falstaff from the royal court , sometimes ending a friendship is a sign of the maturity necessary to lead
Barack Obama made just such a choice in 2008 after the hateful and conspiratorial remarks of his longtime pastor, Jeremiah Wright, were exposed to the world
Obama’s relationship with Wright was much more intimate than that between El-Sayed and Piker or Vance and Carlson; he had sat in Wright’s pews for decades, and Wright had baptized his children

And yet Obama ultimately turned his back on Wright, saying that the preacher’s divisive, anti-American “rants” were “an insult to what we’ve been trying to do in this campaign.” Obama understood that as long as he was associated with a character like Wright, he could never be a credible advocate for the national unity he claimed to seek

title: The Book Claiming to Teach Couples How to Select Their Baby’s Sex
excerpt: When Christina Kattula, a 31-year-old yoga teacher in Michigan, was ready to start a family in 2024, she hoped for a son
body: When Christina Kattula, a 31-year-old yoga teacher in Michigan, was ready to start a family in 2024, she hoped for a son

Her husband “wanted a boy to bond with,” she told me. “And if we had girls later, he thought it would be cute to have a protective-big-brother-type thing.” Kattula decided to try something she’d heard about on a podcast: the so-called Babydust Method

The theory, which was first laid out in a self-published book from 2016, claims, contrary to scientific evidence, that couples can influence their baby’s sex by precisely timing when they have intercourse
What’s the harm if it doesn’t work? Kattula and her husband followed the book’s advice, and she became pregnant with a boy
During her pregnancy, Kattula posted a TikTok to her few hundred followers recommending the book to other couples. “Blessed either way,” she said in the video . “But it worked for us

If you’re on your last kid and you’re really, really trying for something, read The Babydust Method .” She’s one of many women on TikTok and elsewhere on social media who credit Babydust with helping them conceive a child of their preferred sex

Some acknowledge that the method is scientifically unfounded, while other posters are more credulous: In one video, Julie Wise, a mom of two in Massachusetts, said that it’s “not like a fact; I’m pretty sure it’s just like a theory,” but that she is nevertheless “kind of a believer.” In Wisconsin, a day-care owner and mom of four named Courtney Raspor said the method has something like a “90 percent success rate.” Some go a step beyond what the book recommends, into the realm of the woo: In Australia, Faye Briotti said that in addition to timing when she had sex, she also kept pink crystals and salt by her bed, and painted her nails pink

A woman named Reagan, who’d had two boys and was hoping for a girl, said that she got rid of all her baby boy clothes , “because I really wanted to put out into the universe that I wanted a girl.” [ Read: The best parenting hack is being rich ] The rise of TikTok and other social-media platforms has given audiences ready access to folk-science life hacks of all kinds

People can now more quickly find vertical videos about scientifically suspect practices such as mouth-taping and cortisol-lowering than they can make a doctor’s appointment to address snoring or weight gain
Conceiving and carrying a pregnancy—high-stakes experiences that are full of uncertainty—seem to make some women unusually susceptible to dubious strategies
Kathryn Taylor, the author of The Babydust Method , got the idea when she was preparing to conceive her first child
She wanted to see if she could increase her odds of having a boy—she thought her husband would be more excited about the baby if it was
She is not a medical doctor and doesn’t have a Ph.D.; she has a bachelor’s degree in microbiology, immunology, and molecular genetics, and now works in pharmaceutical sales

But she knew that an embryo’s sex is determined by the sperm that takes part in creating it: If the sperm carries a Y chromosome, the embryo will be a boy; if it has an X chromosome, the embryo will be a girl
And so she wondered if she could encourage a Y-bearing sperm to fertilize her egg

She read studies about reproduction on PubMed, a medical database, and came away believing that, after a man and woman have sex, Y sperm undergo an activation process called capacitation faster than X sperm do, but that they also deteriorate sooner
Therefore, she posited, having sex as close as possible to the day the woman ovulates should give boy sperm the best chance of getting to the egg first
By the same logic, having sex a few days before ovulation would allow the boy sperm time to die off before the egg arrives, and increase the likelihood that an X sperm will fertilize the egg

Sandra Carson, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist at Yale who has written about sex-selection efforts since the 1980s, and Michael Zinaman, a reproductive endocrinologist in New York, told me that X and Y sperm don’t move or activate at different rates, that one doesn’t live longer than the other, and that the timing or frequency of intercourse does not determine the fetus’s sex
Taylor told me she was “100 percent” sure the method was going to work for her

As she writes in her author bio, she had “a boy first and a girl second, just like she planned.” She decided to write the book, she told me, after a few moms who had “three boys or whatever” asked her how she had managed to get one child of each sex, and after she shared her tips, she said, they were successful too
She set out to create a short, readable guide—the Kindle version of Babydust is 82 pages long—to help other women

Taylor has claimed that the method works about 87 percent of the time; more than 50,000 people now belong to a Babydust Method Facebook group, which requires proof of book purchase—$10 on Amazon—to join. [ From the September 2026 issue: The great romance slump ] When I asked Taylor about Carson and Zinaman’s research, she stuck by her theory

She told me that doctors might not understand the method because they work with patients rather than researching sperm. (Carson has researched sperm extensively.) Taylor emphasized that she thinks a crucial difference between X and Y sperm is their capacitation, and even if that’s proved wrong, she said, it “doesn’t debunk the theory.” It would just mean, she believes, that male and female sperm are distinct in a way “that’s microscopic, that’s genetic, and it’s deep inside the cell.” Attempts to naturally influence a baby’s sex have a long history
Hippocrates believed that having intercourse immediately after a woman’s period would increase the odds of conceiving a son; doing so “a good while” later, he thought, would favor a girl
In the 1960s, an ob-gyn named Landrum Shettles hypothesized that Y sperm are faster but more fragile, and that to conceive a boy, a couple should have sex as close to ovulation as possible
The following decade, a public-health researcher named Elizabeth Whelan proposed entirely different advice: that couples seeking to conceive a boy should have sex four to six days before ovulation
Babydust is the updated, Millennial-pink gloss on some of these old ideas
In her book, Taylor argues that although the essence of the Shettles method is correct, the science behind it was wrong
The reality is that none of these ideas are proved to work, and neither is Babydust
At least, they don’t have a better success rate than the 50 or so percent chance a couple has of conceiving either a boy or girl anyway
Zinaman said that if techniques such as Babydust were sound, ob-gyns and fertility doctors would tell patients about them

But, he said, “we don’t have anything we can use to assist patients that way.” The only process that can guarantee having a boy or a girl is in vitro fertilization, which allows parents-to-be to choose the sex of the embryo that gets transferred into the mother. (American doctors are allowed, but not encouraged , to offer IVF for non-medically-necessary sex selection.) This is now such settled science that the most recent definitive study on the topic is from 1995, when researchers recruited 221 women who wanted to become pregnant, tracked their hormones and dates of intercourse, and found that “the timing of sexual intercourse in relation to ovulation has no influence on the sex of the baby.” The author of that study, Allen Wilcox, who once led the Reproductive Epidemiology Group at the National Institutes of Health, told me that no further studies have been conducted about these methods because “you can’t get a paper published saying there’s no association, because every scientist knows that.” [ Read: The problem with child-led potty training ] One reason some people might believe that Babydust is worth trying, despite the lack of evidence, is that it offers a sense of control

All the stages of bringing a baby into the world—trying to conceive, being pregnant, delivering the child, caring for a newborn—can inspire magical thinking in some parents, precisely because so much is out of their hands

One study of hundreds of women undergoing fertility treatments found that 40 percent of them performed a good-luck ritual on the day of their procedure; another, of pregnant Jewish women in Israel, found that they scrupulously avoided buying baby furniture before the baby’s birth in order to avoid “tempting fate.” When my son was still breech at 37 weeks of pregnancy—when most babies have already flipped into the head-down birthing position—my ob-gyn recommended a website of the most batty methods imaginable to get him to rotate

This is how I, a skeptical science writer, found myself standing on my head in a swimming pool one morning and having a “heart to heart” with my fetus about the importance of turning. (This did not work.) It doesn’t help that the first question people typically ask a mother-to-be— Are you having a boy or girl? —is something she has no power over

Many Babydust adherents with whom I spoke and whose videos I watched didn’t seem to believe in Babydust as much as they wanted to believe in something . “People are hoping to alter fate,” Zinaman said, “and half the time it alters fate and they’re happy, and the other half, Oh well, it was never 100 percent anyway .” It can’t hurt to try was something I heard often

Raspor, the Wisconsin day-care owner who used Babydust to conceive a girl, told me, “There’s no way to know whether it was the method or simply chance,” but, “I personally don’t see the harm in giving it a try, as long as you understand that there are no guarantees.” At other points in history, and in certain cultures, many parents hoped for a boy rather than a girl
Today, though, that broad preference seems to have shifted

The Economist reported last year that American and some European couples who have a girl first are more likely to stop at one child than couples who have a boy first, and that adoptive parents are willing to pay a premium for a girl

title: The Download: investigating deaths at the US border’s “virtual wall”
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
The US spent billions on border surveillance

Why can’t it catch people before they die? When José Morales Bernal crossed the border into the US in April 2024, the day before his 32nd birthday, he was within range of three surveillance towers equipped with cameras and AI to automatically detect and track people
If the system worked as intended, Morales should have been apprehended
If he needed medical help, agents were trained to provide it
Instead, Morales died just 360 feet from the closest tower
It was local landfill workers, rather than Border Patrol, who first spotted him
An autopsy concluded that he had died of “environmental exposure.” A first-of-its-kind investigation by MIT Technology Review reveals that deaths like Morales’s are startlingly common

After mapping nearly 4,000 locations where human remains were found against information on nearly 600 surveillance towers, we discovered that a humanitarian crisis at the border has unfolded in view of the government’s own cameras

Read our full investigation into the deadly failings of the virtual wall . —James O’Donnell and Eileen Guo Learn more: As part of our 15-month investigation, we created the first comprehensive map of deaths near US-Mexico border surveillance towers
Take a look at that map , and read about how we made it

The US government is about to spend another $1 billion to triple the virtual wall’s size, yet we found it has systemic flaws: broken towers, algorithms that failed to detect people and agents who simply did not respond to alerts
Here are four ideas for what Customs and Border Protection should do to rectify those failures
An analysis by the Times of San Diego found at least 138 cases since 2022 in which migrants’ remains were found within the nominal range of a nearby surveillance tower
A separate MIT Technology Review analysis estimated that more than half of those people were likely within a tower’s field of view
Here’s her story, written by our partners at Times of San Diego
All of these stories are part of Dying on Camera , our new series investigating the failures of border surveillance technology and their human cost

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 An AI hallucination nearly triggered a US military operation A false report prompted plans to intercept a Chinese vessel. title: How we made the first comprehensive map of deaths along the US border’s “virtual wall”
excerpt: Our 15-month investigation into death and surveillance along the US-Mexico border began with a simple question: Why did so many people die near government surve
body: Our 15-month investigation into death and surveillance along the US-Mexico border began with a simple question: Why did so many people die near government surveillance towers meant to help track and apprehend them? This story is part of  Dying on Camera , a collaboration between  MIT Technology Review  and  Times of San Diego
Journalists in both newsrooms spent the past year examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands

To answer that question, we looked through thousands of pages of government documents, visited the border multiple times, and interviewed more than 45 people, including current and former White House advisors, presidential appointees, Border Patrol agents, medical examiners, sheriffs, humanitarian volunteers, and employees of tech companies
The result of our investigation is the first comprehensive map and analysis of deaths near border surveillance towers
Here’s how we built it, what decisions we made along the way, and what the data can and can’t tell us
Our data The investigation relied on knowing where migrants have died and where and when US Customs and Border Protection towers were installed
We analyzed cases dating back to 2015, allowing us to cover different border policies, presidential administrations, and tower technologies

Migrant deaths The US-Mexico border has been called the world’s deadliest land border, and Border Patrol estimates that more than 10,000 people have died during crossings since 2000—a figure that’s widely considered an undercount
But the amount of information available publicly on where and when these people died, and who they were, varies widely
Some remains are never discovered, and for those that are, there’s no national protocol for how the records are handled

We considered a case for further analysis if we could confirm three basic things: whether the person was believed to have been crossing the border, where the remains were found, and roughly when the person died.  We created our dataset by merging existing ones that had been compiled and shared by other organizations, including No More Deaths, Humane Borders, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation, with new records we obtained ourselves from more than a dozen agencies
Public records requests in Texas Texas was the biggest missing link in most existing databases of migrant deaths
Unlike Arizona, it has no initiative to share records online, and unlike New Mexico, it leaves individual counties to handle their own death investigations

Some records for those individual counties existed, compiled by a handful of dedicated researchers, but nothing was comprehensive or current.  We identified 17 counties in Texas that would be relevant to our investigation: Culberson, Jeff Davis, Presidio, Terrell, Val Verde, Kinney, Maverick, Dimmit, Webb, Zapata, Jim Hogg, Starr, Hidalgo, Cameron, Kenedy, Brooks, and Duval
There are other counties in which migrants have died, but they do not have areas covered by surveillance towers and were therefore excluded
In most of these counties, locally elected administrative judges called justices of the peace collect the most comprehensive information on local deaths
But records requests submitted to these individual judges can stall for years (indeed, some of our requests to justices of the peace remain unfilled more than a year after we filed them)

Reports from justices of the peace sometimes leave out the scene or location details we needed; some justices never even visit the place where a migrant died, instead formally declaring the person deceased over FaceTime with the first responders on scene
The border wall between Sunland Park, New Mexico and Puerto de Anapra, Mexico
GETTY IMAGES MIT Technology Review instead filed records requests to the sheriffs of these 17 counties beginning in July 2025
These agencies are often first on the scene when a death is discovered, and their reports can have more detailed information on where remains were found
But relying on sheriffs’ records means our analysis undercounts migrant deaths in Texas, as it doesn’t include any deaths handled by local or state police
After we filed a request, it took periods of near daily calls to the offices to receive the records, if we received them at all
Other counties charged between $300 and $1,300 to fill our request
Counties warned that their records were incomplete, with an unknown number lost during a move, damaged, destroyed, or misplaced during transitions between sheriffs
Those delays were compounded because most agencies do not record whether a person is believed to have been crossing the border when they died

That’s despite provisions in some counties that allow officers to track far more granular details about other situations; Zapata County reports have a checkbox to indicate whether jewels were stolen in a burglary, for example, while Cameron County reports have one for whether a burglar entered through a chimney
Without a way to readily identify migrant deaths, offices had to pull records by hand, making the process slower, more costly, and more prone to error
We received usable records from 14 of these counties (records have yet to be received from Dimmit or Duval, and Maverick’s office charged a per-record fee that was cost prohibitive)
Agencies generally sent us police reports for each individual case, amounting to over 4,000 pages of records in total
Some were handwritten documents.  Except for the reports from Kenedy, Webb, and Hidalgo Counties, we pulled out the relevant information by hand

For those three counties, which sent large volumes of records, we used Anthropic’s Claude, accessed via API, to inspect each case report and pull out coordinates of the spots where remains were found; then we checked batches of those cases by hand to verify the AI’s accuracy
Agencies sent us records on a rolling basis from July 2025 to February 2026, and most did not specify the date through which their records were current
We generally trusted that agencies sent us cases they believed involved migrant deaths, since they had the most information about each case
But some records clearly suggested otherwise (indicating, for example, that someone died at home), and we excluded those cases
Several hundred cases were removed from our analysis because they didn’t include enough information for us to be certain where the remains were found

In fewer than 100 cases, coordinates were not listed but the description was specific enough for us to locate a point within 0.25 miles of where they were found—so we kept those in.  Compared with agencies in other states along the border, those in Texas provide far fewer details regarding how long ago someone may have died before remains were found or how far the decomposition of those remains had progressed
Some reports included this information, but many didn’t
While autopsy records sometimes have more details, many migrant autopsies in south Texas are done through the Webb County Medical Examiner, which charges a fee for each report
That was cost prohibitive given the scale of our analysis

title: 4 ways to address the failures we found along the US border’s “virtual wall”
excerpt: MIT Technology Review today published our investigation into how many people have died near the “virtual wall” of surveillance towers that the US government has
body: MIT Technology Review today published our investigation into how many people have died near the “virtual wall” of surveillance towers that the US government has installed along the US-Mexico border
We found cases of people who walked undetected through areas surveilled by advanced, AI-enabled towers and later died nearby, where their bodies remained unnoticed for weeks or months
These cases reflect systemic flaws in the virtual wall: broken towers, algorithms that failed to detect people, and agents who simply did not respond to alerts
This story is part of  Dying on Camera , a collaboration between  MIT Technology Review  and  Times of San Diego
Journalists in both newsrooms spent the past year examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands
Each of these deaths should have raised alarms inside US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) about the flaws in the agency’s surveillance network

This is particularly true for cases near the latest towers built by the defense company Anduril, which continues to win major contracts and is poised to benefit from the windfall of federal money slated for border security
The US is set to spend $1 billion to triple the size of the virtual wall by 2034
Here are four ideas for what CBP should do next to address these failures.  1

Conduct a comprehensive audit of deaths near the virtual wall In this June 16, 2021, file photo, a family from Venezuela moves to a Border Patrol transport vehicle after they and other migrants crossed the U.S.-Mexico border and turned themselves in to agents in Del Rio, Texas

ERIC GAY/AP PHOTO “If I were the federal government, I would do an audit, because this feels like it’s not working.”  That was New Mexico state representative Sarah Silva’s reaction when MIT Technology Review showed her that in 2024 alone, more than 18 people had died near surveillance towers in just one small stretch of desert near her district

An audit is necessary because, despite poring over thousands of pages of police reports and other documents about surveillance towers, we have only limited knowledge of how many towers are out there and where they’re located.  CBP does not publish a comprehensive map of its virtual wall

We instead relied on mapping work led by the nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation and then used satellite imagery to verify where specific towers were and approximately when they were installed.  We analyzed lots of towers—nearly 600
But that’s still far less than the 800 the government says operate today
And our estimates of when they went up are inexact
That means our tally of more than 1,050 people who have died near them is an undercount
And we don’t have a complete picture of where along the border the problem is worst
An internal audit would not have such limitations
In theory, CBP tracks when each tower went up and when it was active
It has had the ability to audit their effectiveness—while quantifying how many people have died near them—since at least 2015, when it began installing the types of towers included in our analysis
But sources told us it has never done such an audit
Our findings make the need for one more urgent. 2
Fix the way the agency tracks migrant deaths and remains If CBP is to analyze instances where people have died near its surveillance technology, it needs to know when and where those deaths happen
And the current system for tracking that data is beyond broken
As we note in our methodology , there is no national agency that collects and publishes all available records on migrant deaths

We sifted through thousands of pages of records from dozens of agencies in Texas alone, and our picture is still incomplete owing to the lack of a shared protocol for documenting these deaths in public records.  Border Patrol has had its own internal system, called the Border Safety Initiative Tracking System (BSITS), in place since 2007
But it wasn’t until 2021 that national rules were established for how different sectors should enter cases into the system
The next year, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that many cases still weren’t being tracked in this system, especially deaths that weren’t discovered by Border Patrol
In 2023, the GAO reported that Border Patrol has taken steps to fix that, but outside researchers consistently find the agency’s estimates to be undercounts even today
In addition to tracking migrant deaths, CBP launched a program in 2017 to prevent them, called the Missing Migrant Program
In April 2025, the GAO found the program was improving the way it collected and tracked data about events like 911 calls and rescues
The problem, it said, was that there was no plan in place to use the data to measure whether the program was actually increasing rescues or reducing deaths, which are its primary goals
It made two recommendations for solutions, neither of which has been implemented. 3

Track cases when surveillance technology leads to an apprehension In 2014, when the virtual wall was much smaller, the GAO suggested that Border Patrol agents log when a piece of technology helped them apprehend someone who was trying to enter the US illegally
It would take agents some extra time, but logging these assists would help Congress understand how often various surveillance technologies were leading to actual apprehensions
Once this data was collected, GAO added, the agency should measure whether its surveillance technologies were working
CBP agreed, and it started requiring agents to enter such information
Border Patrol agents apprehend people crossing the border illegally near Sunland Park, N.M., July 17, 2024

GLENN FAWCETT / CBP PHOTO Then, in 2017, the GAO reported that the data being collected was inaccurate and unreliable; it found agents in Texas, for example, who were crediting a specific type of tower in apprehensions hundreds of times, even though no such towers existed anywhere in the state
Border Patrol again said it would improve; it agreed to train agents on the importance of collecting such information

title: The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die?
excerpt: When José Morales Bernal crossed the border into the United States on April 8, 2024, the day before his 32nd birthday, it should have triggered a chain of techn
body: When José Morales Bernal crossed the border into the United States on April 8, 2024, the day before his 32nd birthday, it should have triggered a chain of technological alerts and human responses.  As he walked through the desert in southern New Mexico that morning, he was within range of three surveillance towers
Newly installed by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), they were built by the defense tech company Anduril and equipped with cameras and AI to automatically detect and track people
They transmit live video to nearby control rooms and can send alerts to the government-issued smartphones held by agents in the area, prompting the closest available to respond
This story is part of  Dying on Camera , a collaboration between  MIT Technology Review  and  Times of San Diego
Journalists in both newsrooms spent the past year examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands
These AI-enabled towers are meant to give greater visibility across the 1,951-mile southern border, freeing up border agents from having to spend hours staring into video monitors
They were installed in this particular place to spot border crossers before they reached the nearby town of Sunland Park
If the system worked as intended, Morales should have been apprehended
If he needed medical help, agents were trained to provide it
The view from where José Morales Bernal’s body was found toward a Customs and Border Protection surveillance tower made by Anduril, along the southern US border in Sunland Park, New Mexico
Despite the nearby surveillance towers, it was employees of the local landfill, rather than Border Patrol, who first spotted Morales that morning
At 1 p.m. the workers saw him again, now lying in the sand
At 4 p.m. the landfill workers saw that he had not moved and called Border Patrol

When an agent then called 911 to report the body, he said it was “probably one of the migrants crossing through there,” seemingly unaware that Morales had been moving near the agency’s surveillance systems earlier that day.  The agent can be heard sounding unsure of Morales’ location despite the proximity of an AI-powered surveillance camera
Morales had died just 360 feet from the closest surveillance tower
Two more towers stood watch to the east and the west

An autopsy later concluded that he had died of “environmental exposure.”  The towers surrounding Morales were only the latest addition to the “virtual wall” the government has spent 25 years and billions of dollars building along the entire border, which also includes earlier generations of towers with more basic features, as well as blimps, drones, seismic sensors, and even tunnel-sensing robots

Together, all this technology provides “persistent surveillance” and “situational awareness” to help the Border Patrol quickly and accurately detect people crossing and, crucially, make sure agents are sent to intercept them
CBP has also credited it with saving lives
But a first-of-its-kind investigation by MIT Technology Review reveals that deaths like Morales’s are startlingly common

We cross-referenced nearly 4,000 locations where human remains were found—drawn from records collected by nonprofit groups like No More Deaths and Humane Borders, as well as hundreds of records we obtained in Texas—with information on nearly 600 towers identified by the Electronic Frontier Foundation
We considered when towers were installed and when each person is estimated to have died, and combined this information with field reporting from the border

The result is the first comprehensive map and analysis of deaths near CBP surveillance towers.  Our investigation shows that a humanitarian crisis at the border has unfolded in view of the government’s own cameras
José Morales Bernal died the day before his 32nd birthday
PHOTO COURTESY MIREYA MORALES We found more than 1,050 people who died within range of border surveillance towers between 2015 and early 2026
These deaths are not failures of a few towers or technologies: We found deaths within the advertised range of nearly two-thirds of all the towers we analyzed

Our topographical analysis—which assessed the degree to which terrain might block a tower’s view of a particular death and its surveillance area in general—found that some have sight of as little as 10% of their advertised surveillance area, and yet we also found most deaths did not occur in towers’ blind spots

These deaths are not the result of legacy systems, as our estimate found more than 110 people have died within range of modern autonomous towers from Anduril, among the most advanced systems CBP has deployed, since 2021

The overall picture reveals repeated failures of one of the virtual wall’s basic security functions, as CBP has described it in press releases: to effectively identify and locate migrants entering illegally into the United States.  The year that Morales died, 18 other people died in that same stretch of desert in range of the three Anduril towers
Five were visible from the same surveillance tower closest to where his body was discovered

One man, after walking a mile past the border and in range of two AI towers, dragged his 30-year-old brother into the shade when he began having trouble breathing, according to records we obtained from the medical examiner
The two were spotted by Border Patrol only when the man waved down a helicopter for help; by the time agents arrived, his brother was already dead
A 24-year-old woman died near another Anduril tower, where our terrain analysis showed it should have had clear sight of her location

Her body lay unnoticed for weeks; it was decomposed, and blistered by the summer heat, when it was spotted by agents patrolling the area.  A few miles west, and a short drive from a Border Patrol station, four other AI towers stood watch
Near them, 10 more bodies were found that year, all in locations where at least one tower had a clear view
In response to a list of questions, an Anduril spokesperson replied that once a tower is delivered, it is operated by CBP, and directed questions about specific incidents to the agency

The response noted that an incident occurring nearby does not mean the tower missed a detection and said actual surveillance ranges vary depending on terrain, physical obstructions, and the boundaries CBP sets for where the tower should look (CBP is able to set virtual boundaries on towers’ views for privacy and other reasons)
The Anduril spokesperson also alleged inaccuracies in our reporting, given those boundaries and obstructions, but did not respond to follow-up questions on what was inaccurate
The most pressing question in any death near the virtual wall is whether authorities knew someone was there and failed to reach them or weren’t aware anyone was crossing at all
And the deaths we found capture only the failures that left a trace—we don’t know how many people pass through undetected, or how many bodies remain undiscovered

title: She died at the San Diego border. A surveillance camera was in plain sight
excerpt: She had only walked for a couple of hours, and already she was lost.  It was early afternoon on Sept. 14, 2025, when 30-year-old Graciela Gómez Hernández c
body: She had only walked for a couple of hours, and already she was lost.  It was early afternoon on Sept. 14, 2025, when 30-year-old Graciela Gómez Hernández crossed the border from the eastern edge of Tijuana into Southern California, sending voice messages to her mother and sister as she walked.  This story is part of  Dying on Camera , a collaboration between  MIT Technology Review  and  Times of San Diego
Journalists in both newsrooms spent the past year examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands
Gómez Hernández did not tell her family about her plan until the day before
Once she arrived in California, she hoped to work and send money back to her three children and her parents in southern Mexico
Her oldest son, age 11, had asked for a bicycle.   She either climbed a ladder over the border wall or slipped through a section in steep terrain where fencing has yet to be built
Dozens of game trails cut through the dust on hillsides of sagebrush and manzanita

It was the first segment of a hike through the Otay Mountain Wilderness.  The eastern edge of San Diego is just a mile away, but countless migrants hike 10 or 20 miles north through the mountains to evade the Border Patrol, emerging in smaller towns and on distant highways with fewer checkpoints
A border agent rides an ATV along the U.S.-Mexico border outside San Diego, September 2026
While the mountainous terrain makes some areas difficult to access, the area is blanketed with interconnected surveillance technology

ANNIE BARKER/TIMES OF SAN DIEGO/CATCHLIGHT LOCAL/REPORT FOR AMERICA Between 2 and 3 p.m., her sister said, Gómez Hernández sent a final message to her mother. “I can’t do it anymore,” she whispered into her phone
By the time a forensic crew came to collect her, two weeks later, most of her body had disappeared into the earth.  She died on her own, but she was not, strictly speaking, alone
She was in one of the most heavily surveilled strips of land in the world
Before she died, Gómez Hernández told her family in a WhatsApp message that she could see helicopters overhead and white Border Patrol trucks making periodic laps on the road below
And even if none of those agents saw her or knew she was in distress, something else had a clear view

Supervising the whole territory, from a nearby hilltop, was a slender gray surveillance tower.  That tower, made by General Dynamics and in place since 2019, boasts two sets of electro-optical and infrared cameras with long-range lenses that can track targets 5 to 7 miles away

Gómez Hernández was just one mile away.  Surveillance towers have proliferated in recent years, as contractors added newer camera systems that use artificial intelligence to distinguish border-crossers from other people and animals, and track their movements, at an overall cost of more than a billion dollars.  Yet as the cameras scan the terrain, migrants continue to die in plain sight.  Thousands of migrants have died while crossing the border in the past two decades, many of them near to Border Patrol surveillance installations

But the phenomenon is especially pronounced in the Otay Mountain Wilderness, just outside San Diego.  A Times of San Diego analysis counted hundreds of cases along the California border—including at least 138 in the past four years—where migrants’ remains were found within the range of the very cameras designed to help track and intercept them.  A topographical analysis conducted as part of an MIT Technology Review investigation estimated that more than half of these remains were found in a spot where a camera would have a clear view of a person, without terrain blocking the line of sight.  Some of these migrants died swiftly, falling from the border wall or drowning in a canal or river

But dozens suffered slow deaths of exposure in the wilderness, deaths that might have been averted with emergency aid.  People who died in Southern California came from just across the border, or from as far away as Africa
But they all died within range of a surveillance camera
Found in July 2023: Marcia Dutra, a 36-year-old woman from Brazil who likely died of heat exposure next to a border fence
According to a medical examiner’s report, a group of migrants told the Border Patrol about her body when they were apprehended

An AI-equipped surveillance tower sits 2,000 feet northeast above the edge of a plateau, out of sight of the slope where she was found.  Found in February 2024: Elvi Vasquez Bortolon, a 28-year-old Mexican man who died of suspected hypothermia on a ridge near the border wall
He had been dead for more than five days when a Border Patrol agent in a helicopter spotted his body from above

A remote video tower stands about 1,400 feet away, hidden from view by the ridge above the canyon.  Found in August 2024: Ramón Montenegro, a 51-year-old man from Mexico who died of possible heatstroke in the mountains near Dulzura

An AI surveillance tower, invisible on the other side of a hill, sits 1,300 feet away — roughly the length of the parking lot at the San Diego Zoo.  More than 120 surveillance towers stand along the California border, according to documents and live observations collected by the Electronic Frontier Foundation.  The towers are not the only form of surveillance in the region
The border is blanketed by an interconnected network of trail cameras, underground movement detectors, radar, infrared sensors, drones, and even blimps

In March 2025, the Trump administration directed the Department of Defense to use satellites to watch the border as well.  Even when mountains or vegetation block a tower’s view, other devices may pick up the trail
Local advocates say surveillance technology in the Otay Mountain Wilderness is almost unavoidable.  Agents in Border Patrol gear hike a ridge in the Otay Mountain Wilderness, September 2026
Agents said the group was on a training hike

ANNIE BARKER/TIMES OF SAN DIEGO/CATCHLIGHT LOCAL/REPORT FOR AMERICA Officials say the towers particularly excel at tracking passing migrants.  Anduril, the company that makes about half the towers now installed at the U.S.-Mexico border, said in a news release in 2024 that their towers “directly contributed to saving lives and stopping illicit drugs from entering the U.S.” In June 2026, the company said its installations had “autonomously identified hundreds of thousands of border crossings.” John Morris, a Border Patrol sector chief in Arizona, told media at a convention in May 2026 that “We’re dang close to pretty much knowing everything that comes across.”  The proximity of so many deaths to high-resolution cameras leaves two distinct possibilities: Either the system didn’t detect these people in distress, or it did detect them—and officials offered no response.  Anduril, the defense contracting company that manufactures the AI-enabled towers, did not respond to questions from Times of San Diego about the towers’ performance in mountainous terrain

A representative of General Dynamics, which made the tower closest to Gómez Hernández’s body, referred all questions to the Border Patrol.  The Border Patrol did not respond to questions from Times of San Diego regarding whether surveillance towers spotted Gómez Hernández prior to her death, or about how surveillance cameras in general are used to detect people in emergency situations.  Rafael Hernández Larraenza, the leader of a search and rescue group, Desert Angels, says he believes some of the towers are “just adornment,” and are not actually effective at tracking migrants

He also says that Border Patrol agents, in occasional meetings with his search group, “say they don’t have the opportunity to do searches, that they don’t have enough time.” People in need of rescue “are not a priority,” said Bryce Peterson, who compiles research on migrant remains for the advocacy group No More Deaths.  A wilderness, heavily watched   From the spot where Graciela Gómez Hernández’s body was found, a surveillance tower stands in clear view.  That tower is one mile away
A second, newer tower, on the other side of a hill, sits 1.4 miles away
Both are equipped with slow-spinning, long-range cameras.  The closer of these two towers is situated between two layers of border fencing, a long pole, over 100 feet tall, reaching into the sky

It peers not only onto hillsides where migrants walk, but into the brightly-colored cinderblock homes of a Tijuana neighborhood.  The second tower is much shorter, just 33 feet tall, surveying the canyon where Gómez Hernández would most likely have arrived if she had kept walking.  This new tower, built by a company called Anduril, decides for itself whether a moving object in the field is relevant
The two dark, round cameras on the pole give the impression of eyes, rotating slowly, and then locking in on a target, before swiveling elsewhere
Federal cameras seen at Friendship Park in San Diego, September 2026

ANNIE BARKER/TIMES OF SAN DIEGO/CATCHLIGHT LOCAL/REPORT FOR AMERICA Osvaldo Ruiz, the volunteer coordinator for the Border Angels, a group that leaves water and supplies along migrant trails near San Diego, says the Otay Mountain wilderness has “beacons throughout the mountains” that “can see over a lot of the mountains facing the border.” “At entry sites that migrants or travelers may come through, there are also hidden cameras inside of rocks or inside of bushes that are camouflaged for you not to see
And then there’s also the cameras that you see on the road

They have license plate readers that are stuck on the back of a safety cone, so (it detects) as you’re driving away from it.” Surveillance towers have been in the area since 2011, with frequent new installations, including the introduction of AI-directed towers in 2018

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760977/original/file-20260920-50-4g0cza.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption"> MS NOW White House Correspondent Akayla Gardner prepares to report from a street corner outside the White House grounds after being denied entry on Sept. 19, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/white-house-correspondent-akayla-gardner-prepares-for-a-news-photo/2295495512?adppopup=true">Graeme Sloan/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The president is going after the press again.</p>

<p>On Sept. 19, 2026, journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico were denied access to the White House <a href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-ban-ms-now-media-cnn-politico-72f9acf68244ca70e9078d9d3661c722">after President Donald Trump revoked their credentials</a>, citing “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” On social media, Trump posted, “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117293599348325006">when they’re covering the President</a>.”</p>

<p><a href="https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/post/a-roundup-of-donald-trump-actions-against-the-press/?utm_source=substack&amp;utm_medium=email">This is not Trump’s first attempt</a> at banning journalists from the White House. <a href="https://www.npr.org/2018/11/13/667425530/cnn-sues-trump-administration-over-jim-acostas-press-credentials">During his first term</a>, he sought to ban CNN’s Jim Acosta by revoking his credentials <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2018/11/13/business/media/cnn-jim-acosta-trump-lawsuit.html">following a contentious news conference</a> about the 2018 midterm elections. </p>

<p>In that conflict, CNN quickly filed a lawsuit, arguing that, “If left unchallenged, the actions of the White House would create a dangerous chilling effect for <a href="https://www.politico.com/story/2018/11/13/cnn-sues-trump-administration-985747">any journalist who covers our elected officials</a>.”</p>

<p>Journalism organizations also responded. The Committee to Protect Journalists, the Radio Television Digital News Association and even Acosta’s peers at The Daily Caller – a right-leaning news outlet – <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2018/11/08/media/trump-acosta-press-pass-reaction/index.html">condemned the White House ban</a>. </p>

<p>A federal court <a href="https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/cnn-gets-temporary-due-process-ruling-in-trump-case">granted CNN a temporary injunction</a> – reinstating Acosta’s press pass. The <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/cnn-drops-suit-against-white-house-after-acostas-press-pass-is-fully-restored/2018/11/19/519763fc-ec3a-11e8-8679-934a2b33be52_story.html">Trump administration later restored Acosta’s credentials</a>, and CNN dropped its lawsuit.</p>

<p>Many commentators and members of the press have called Trump’s latest ban on the three news organizations <a href="https://www.facebook.com/ABCNews/videos/first-amendment-battle-brewing-over-white-house-access/1083884914050614/">a violation of the First Amendment</a>.</p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Donald Trump’s Sept. 18, 2026, social media post announcing he was banning the three news organizations from the White House.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006">Truth Social Donald Trump account</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich said on X, “Today’s action revoking access for journalists from CNN, POLITICO, and MSNOW <a href="https://x.com/whca/status/2101371576403050530">violates the First Amendment</a>.” </p>

<p>Even George Washington University law professor Jonathan Turley, who staunchly supports Republicans and frequently criticizes the press, said on X that the ban “<a href="https://x.com/JonathanTurley/status/2101041961499058481?s=20">would be an assault on long-honored principles of a free press</a>.” </p>

<p>As Turley and many others have argued over the weekend, Trump’s ban is almost certainly <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution/first_amendment">unconstitutional under the First Amendment</a>, which states that “Congress shall make no law … abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press.” Media law professor Frank LoMonte argued in 2018, “The First Amendment guarantees all Americans <a href="https://theconversation.com/can-trumps-white-house-legally-ban-reporters-101062">freedom to speak and publish without government interference</a>.” </p>

<p>But they may be missing a crucial point. In fact, there’s more than one constitutional right involved in such a case. The judge who restored Acosta’s press pass in 2018 primarily based his ruling on the reporter’s Fifth Amendment rights to due process, not on the First Amendment.</p>

<p>And in my view as a constitutional law professor, it is less clear whether the press has a constitutional right of access to the White House even though past presidents have honored and respected the press’s access to the executive branch. </p>

<p>While several Supreme Court cases, such as <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/448/555/">Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia</a>, unequivocally provide the press with a right of access to criminal trials, there is no Supreme Court precedent that specifically provides a clear constitutional right of access to the White House. </p>



<h2>Make that two constitutional rights</h2>

<p>In one case from 1977, <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/569/124/35083/">Sherrill v. Knight</a>, Robert Sherrill, the Washington correspondent for The Nation, was – after holding press passes over several years – denied a press pass because the Secret Service advised he should not be given one. The Secret Service refused to disclose their justification. </p>

<p>Sherrill sued, and the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that the Secret Service cannot deny a White House press pass absent “narrow and specific standards by which applications are to be judged.” </p>

<p>The court required the White House to provide the press with “notice of the factual bases for denial, an opportunity for (them) to respond to these, and a final written statement of the reasons for denial (of a press pass).” </p>

<p>In the court’s view, these requirements – notice and an opportunity to rebut the bases for the denial of a press pass – are protected by two constitutional guarantees working together, the press protections in the First Amendment and the <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-5/">Fifth Amendment’s protections</a> from arbitrary deprivations of “life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” </p>

<p>In other words, before the federal government can deprive an individual of their life, liberty or property, the federal government must provide that individual with <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/due_process">due process</a>, whose purpose is widely accepted as preventing “<a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/due-process-law">arbitrary governmental actions</a>.”</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in a suit walking near a white building." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=414&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=520&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=520&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760979/original/file-20260920-60-fg3saf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=520&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
