            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Due process is key</h2>

<p>There are a number of Supreme Court decisions that could be key in the <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754.1.0_1.pdf">current journalists’ lawsuit</a>, which was filed on Sept. 21, 2026.</p>

<p>Among them is <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/424/319/">Mathews v. Eldridge</a> from 1976, in which the Supreme Court stated that due process is flexible depending on the extent of the liberty or property interest at stake. But in general, the justices said, due process requires the government to provide notice to the individual and an opportunity for the individual to present their case before the deprivation occurs. </p>

<p>In <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/569/124/35083/">Sherrill v. Knight</a> from 1977, the court ruled that the denial of a press pass implicated a First Amendment liberty interest. That interest, the court wrote, “undoubtedly qualifies as liberty which may not be denied without due process of law under the fifth amendment.” </p>

<p>This nuance – the First and Fifth Amendment working in tandem – is what most commentators and critics are missing in their response to the recent ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico. In fact, these outlets collectively lead with their claim that the Trump administration violated their Fifth Amendment right to due process in their <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754.1.0_1.pdf">lawsuit to block Trump’s ban</a>.</p>

<p>“Even if attending a White House event is not a constitutionally guaranteed right, that doesn’t mean the government <a href="https://theconversation.com/can-trumps-white-house-legally-ban-reporters-101062">is free to take it away as punishment</a>,” LoMonte argued in 2018. </p>

<p>Based on public reporting, it is clear that the <a href="https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a0-c343-d2df-a1f4-f7cf04bf0000">Trump administration did not provide CNN, MS NOW or Politico with clear written notice stating the reasons for the revocation</a> of their press passes. It certainly did not provide the outlets with an opportunity to rebut Trump’s unsupported claim that they report “FICTION and LIES.” </p>

<p>The same Trump-appointed judge who decided the CNN Acosta case <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/21/timothy-kelly-judge-white-house-ban-lawsuit-01086120">has been assigned to the latest press ban case</a>. So, if the CNN Acosta case is any indication, I expect the federal judge to promptly, but temporarily, reinstate the news outlets’ press passes while Trump tries to argue that his actions are constitutional, which in my view, they are not.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292435/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Three Ts will dominate Trump-Xi summit – but expect little movement on trade, less on Taiwan and who knows on tech</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760975/original/file-20260920-50-a2zbbr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C41%2C2145%2C1429&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping tour Zhongnanhai Garden in Beijing on May 15, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-and-chinese-president-xi-jinping-news-photo/2275740840?adppopup=true">Evan Vucci-Pool/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping <a href="https://theconversation.com/xi-trump-summit-trade-taiwan-and-russia-still-top-agenda-for-china-and-us-presidents-6-years-after-last-meeting-268471">last sat down in May 2026</a>, talk was centered on three Ts: trade, technology and Taiwan. </p>

<p>The latest summit, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/china/trump-plans-greet-xi-arrival-washington-area-officials-say-2026-09-18/">due to begin in the United States on Sept. 24</a>, looks set to focus on the same set of issues again. The main difference will be that the technology element has been given added urgency by the <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/chuckbrooks/2026/03/14/the-rapid-trajectory-of-artificial-intelligence/">sudden and rapid shift</a> in developments in artificial intelligence. </p>

<p>What’s less clear is whether the two sides will be able to come to any sort of transformative agreement on that, or any other issue.</p>

<h2>Tweaks to trade?</h2>

<p>The most urgent issue, but also the simplest to solve, will be on trade. </p>

<p>Nearly <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/what-happened-when-trump-met-xi/">a year ago at Busan in South Korea</a>, Trump and Xi hammered out an agreement whereby the U.S. agreed to lift some export controls on high-end technology and to reduce the then three-figure tariffs on Chinese goods. For its part, China agreed not to restrict the flow of critical minerals and rare earths to U.S. users.</p>

<p>That pact is now up for renewal. Both sides are likely to want a continuation of the current arrangement, and while there may be some tweaking on the side, the new deal will probably be similar to the old one.</p>

<p>Each side has proposed in previous meetings that there should be a new instrument, <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/what-is-the-us-china-board-of-trade-12025405">a Board of Trade</a>, that will assess non-sensitive U.S.-China business interests. </p>

<p>However, details about the institution remains vague. Some announcements are likely during the summit, but business leaders will want to know how comprehensive and lasting the arrangements for the board will be. </p>

<p>There is still less information on a proposed <a href="https://www.scmp.com/news/us/economy-trade-business/article/3363829/us-china-board-investment-stalls-expected-trump-xi-meeting">Board of Investment</a>, which remains on the drawing board. The Chinese side has proposed bringing major Chinese CEOs to the summit to match the likes of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk – both of whom <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5yx757w048o">accompanied Trump on the Beijing trip</a>.</p>

<p>But the choice of business leaders is likely to turn on which aspects of trade China thinks are likely to develop most effectively in the short term.</p>

<h2>The always thorny issue of Taiwan</h2>

<p>Taiwan is a much harder issue to solve, but it’s unlikely that much that is discussed on Xi’s visit will determine its outcome. </p>

<p>Trump has been <a href="https://theconversation.com/biden-on-taiwan-did-he-really-commit-us-forces-to-stopping-any-invasion-by-china-an-expert-explains-why-on-balance-probably-not-176765">less willing than his predecessor to commit</a> the U.S. to defending the island should Beijing invade, instead reasserting Washington’s long-held position of strategic ambiguity.</p>

<p>And although the U.S. is currently distracted from East Asia by the Iran conflict, China still prefers to find methods short of war to bring the island under Beijing’s control. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Men in army fatigues are seen behind barbed-wire." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760978/original/file-20260920-50-t6tqx4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Taiwanese soldiers set up anti-tank obstacles to simulate stopping Chinese forces during the Han-Kuang military exercise on Aug. 6, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/taiwanese-soldiers-set-up-anti-tank-obstacles-on-the-news-photo/2288502963?adppopup=true">Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The island’s <a href="https://atlasinstitute.org/how-the-2028-taiwanese-elections-could-determine-beijings-calculus-in-the-taiwan-strait/">January 2028 presidential election</a> is likely to be a more crucial moment for Taiwan’s future, particularly if the opposition — and more China-friendly — Kuomintang party wins the presidency, or indeed if an isolationist candidate becomes U.S. president later that year. If the next U.S. president opted to change course by taking a less active involvement in overseas issues — as has been floated by early contenders on both the left and right — that would change things all the more.</p>

<p>For now, Beijing will continue to build the People’s Liberation Army’s naval capacity to have the option of military action against the island. But its preference will be to take advantage of changes within Taiwan’s internal politics while combining economic incentives and coercion, squeezing Taipei’s international footprint and hoping for a <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/us-asia-western-pacific-allies-withdrawal-china-defense-graphics/a-79275554">slackening of U.S. interest</a> in the western Pacific.</p>

<p>Other international issues are likely to gain less attention. China is expected to make clear its <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/clyl8965j5go">unhappiness about the war on Iran</a>, and the U.S. may remind China that it has passed new legislation allowing sanctions on countries that buy Russian oil – of which, China is the largest purchaser. However, neither issue is likely to lead to any major change in practice.</p>

<h2>Turning to tech</h2>

<p>It’s really in the area of tech, and AI in particular, where both sides will be trying to make diplomacy catch up with reality. The May summit surprised many because the question of mutual agreement on regulation of AI came up in a way that had not been on the agenda for the first year of the Trump administration.</p>

<p>However, both sides <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/world/asia/china-ai-risks-agree-slowdown-us-tech-rcna597859">agreed that talks in principle about regulation</a> might be possible and even desirable because of the growth in the importance, but also unpredictability, of AI. And on Sept, 20, the U.S. and China mooted the idea of a “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/20/business/us-china-ai-warning-system-national-security.html">hotline” to notify the other</a> over AI national security risks.</p>

<p>Between the May and September summits, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/us/politics/ai-catastrophe-fears-washington.html">fears about AI in the U.S</a> have created an increasingly unfriendly atmosphere toward unregulated AI.</p>

<p>In China, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/opinion/ai-china-america-risk.html">public sentiment about AI is less openly hostile</a> and some of its major benefits in areas such as healthcare have softened people’s attitudes. Yet there are still plenty of concerns expressed in private about whether China’s troubled economy will definitively benefit from the AI boom. Although many argue it has created new opportunities for consumers, others point to the <a href="https://qz.com/china-workers-ai-job-displacement-youth-unemployment-091826">relatively few jobs that have been created</a> for a workforce that finds itself buffeted by wide-scale job elimination.</p>

<p>Both the U.S. and China have reasons to talk about AI regulation. The alarming prospect of rogue AI companies causing intense social disruptions through their business choices is clearly one such reason, and in the U.S., voters’ more <a href="https://www.wpri.com/news/us-and-world/ap-americans-are-increasingly-concerned-about-the-environmental-impact-of-ai-new-poll-finds/">immediate concerns about data centers</a> are another.</p>

<p>There are also China-specific reasons that Beijing may seek restraint. One of the most common concerns about AI is that it may well run out of control. And “out of control” is a kryptonite phrase for the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. That’s particularly true of Xi who, as a youth, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/25/world/asia/xi-jinping-china-cultural-revolution.html">spent years in rural exile</a> after his father fell to a purge just before the Cultural Revolution – an upheaval during which China’s politics turned to anarchy. It was a formative experience for Xi, which has no doubt influenced his tendencies as a leader toward exercising as much control as possible.</p>

<p>AI that undermines the unchallengeable leadership of the Communist Party would be an unwelcome guest in China’s cyberspace, and regulation that solves that problem would not be rejected out of hand.</p>

<p>However, this recognition of mutual concern about AI – albeit for very different reasons – is still not likely to see much progress in the short term. The competition between the U.S. and China on AI is real, and neither governments nor private sector actors in either country are willing to make concessions that could advantage the other side. </p>

<p>Levels of trust between Washington and Beijing <a href="https://fortune.com/2026/09/15/ai-safety-pact-without-us-china-trust/">remain very low on the issue</a>. Talks about talks seem the most likely public outcome, though what happens behind the scenes may be pursued more discreetly.</p>

<h2>It’s good to talk</h2>

<p>The Trump-Xi summit is less important in terms of any major change in policy on either side, and more because it marks part of a commitment to maintain some form of dialogue between the leaders of the world’s two most powerful countries. The leaders may well meet twice more in the near future, at the G20 and APEC summits. </p>

<p>To meet four times in just over half a year is a good sign; refusal to meet would be much more worrying. </p>

<p>But the underlying difficulties of the three Ts, where the leaders seem to have fundamentally incompatible agendas, remain the thread beneath the ostensibly polite and occasionally amiable conversations.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291819/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Noise pollution is a serious but often forgotten public health problem

<title>Noise pollution is a serious but often forgotten public health problem</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756777/original/file-20260828-50-pgx3ag.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7007%2C4672&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Noise pollution is an occupational health hazard for many workers.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/young-woman-working-on-a-drill-press-machine-in-a-royalty-free-image/2166870837?phrase=noise%20at%20work&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">urbazon/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The human body is remarkably good at getting used to the environment around it. You’ve probably experienced this if you’ve ever gone to a matinee and emerged from the dark theater into sunshine. Your eyes sting, so you squint and shield your face until they adjust to the bright sunlight.</p>

<p>In the same way, the body can grow accustomed to constant noise. With repeated exposure to traffic, leaf blowers, construction, loud music, crowded restaurants, fitness classes and sporting events, you can become accustomed to loud environments. Over time, what once seemed unusually loud may barely register.</p>

<p>But what feels normal isn’t necessarily safe. Noise is an important but often overlooked environmental health hazard, with effects ranging from <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21776-noise-induced-hearing-loss-nihl">hearing loss</a> to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/eurpub/ckad044">cardiovascular disease</a>.</p>

<p>I think about noise constantly because <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=yfpAws0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">I’m an audiologist and hearing scientist</a> with expertise in occupational exposures. But hazardous noise isn’t limited to the workplace. You likely encounter noise every day without knowing when it poses a risk. The good news is that many of the harmful effects of noise are preventable – once you know what to listen for.</p>

<h2>Noise affects more than your ears</h2>

<p>The most obvious consequence of excessive noise is <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm12062347">hearing damage</a>. Loud sounds can damage delicate sensory cells in the inner ear, leading to permanent hearing loss. <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/tinnitus/symptoms-causes/syc-20350156">Tinnitus, or ringing in the ears</a>, is another common consequence of noise exposure.</p>

<p>But hearing damage is only part of the story. Chronic environmental noise can affect health through other pathways, too. Noise <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(13)61613-X">acts as a stressor</a>, activating the autonomic nervous and endocrine systems and affecting heart rate, blood pressure and other physiological processes. It can also <a href="https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/43bf485d-2771-4297-86fe-6284430090ef/content">disturb sleep</a>, <a href="https://www.who.int/europe/publications/i/item/9789289053563">triggering stress responses</a> even without fully waking us.</p>

<p>Over months or years, these repeated effects can take a toll on the body. Long-term traffic noise exposure has been linked to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fcvm.2026.1834139">hypertension</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/EE9.0000000000000400">coronary artery disease, stroke</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-023-25926-5">Type 2 diabetes</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/about/noise.html">Workplace noise recommendations</a> are primarily designed to protect workers from hearing loss. In contrast, the World Health Organization’s <a href="https://www.who.int/tools/compendium-on-health-and-environment/environmental-noise/">environmental noise guidelines</a> recommend lower levels because they consider longer exposure periods and broader effects on health.</p>

<p><iframe id="F8Hgz" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/F8Hgz/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="line chart showing safe exposure time to loud noises, where the y axis is time and the x axis is volume"></iframe></p>

<h2>How loud is too loud?</h2>

<p>The risk from noise <a href="https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/how-does-noise-damage-your-hearing">depends on how loud it is</a>, how long you’re exposed and how close you are to the source. Extremely loud sounds, such as fireworks or gunshots, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2018/impulse-noise.html">can damage hearing almost instantly</a>, especially at close range. Other sounds, such as power tools, loud music or heavy traffic, can <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/hearing-loss/causes/">pose a risk more gradually</a>, as exposure adds up over time.</p>

<p>The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommends limiting occupational noise exposure to 85 <a href="https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/A-weighted-decibels-dBA-or-dBa-or-dBa">A-weighted decibels, or dBA</a>, averaged over an eight-hour workday. A-weighting adjusts the measurement to better reflect how the human ear responds to sound. For every 3 dBA increase, the recommended exposure time is cut in half. </p>

<p>Similar benchmarks are used elsewhere: Australia <a href="https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/duties-tool/construction/hazards-information/noise">limits workplace exposure</a> to 85 dBA over 8 hours, while the <a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/LSU/?uri=oj:JOL_2003_042_R_0038_01&amp;">European Union</a> and <a href="https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm">Great Britain</a> require protective measures beginning at 80 dBA and additional measures at 85 dBA, and both prohibit exposure above 87 dBA after accounting for hearing protection. Though regulatory details differ, 85 dBA averaged over eight hours is a widely used international benchmark for occupational noise.</p>

<p>And you don’t get a fresh start each time you leave a noisy environment. Rather, noise exposure adds up over the course of a day. Spending four hours at 88 dBA uses the same maximum recommended daily noise dose as eight hours at 85 dBA. Time spent around loud traffic, using power tools, attending a sporting event or listening to loud music can all contribute to that daily dose.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="man on subway wearing earbuds" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756785/original/file-20260828-50-shhgbf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Over time, exposure to ambient noise from traffic or public transportation can cause long-term health problems.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/solo-traveler-using-subway-train-to-get-around-the-royalty-free-image/1406868509?phrase=person%20with%20earbuds%20train&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How to protect yourself from too much noise</h2>

<p>Protecting your hearing doesn’t necessarily mean avoiding sound altogether. The goal is to manage your daily noise dose. </p>

<p>It helps to start by learning your baseline daily exposure. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health offers a free app called the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/about/app.html">NIOSH sound level meter</a> that can estimate the noise level around you.</p>

<p>When you have a choice, select quieter equipment and environments. When driving, keep your car windows closed in heavy traffic. When you go out to eat, try to choose a table away from noise sources in a loud restaurant.</p>

<p>But if you find yourself in a noisy environment, it’s helpful to take breaks and wear hearing protection whenever possible. <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25662567/">Filtered earplugs</a> reduce sound levels while still allowing you to enjoy music or participate in conversation.</p>

<p>Whenever possible, it’s a good idea to turn down the volume on your headphones. Most smartphones allow you to set an upper limit on audio volume so that you aren’t turning up the volume on your music or podcast to unsafe levels. As the ambient sound increases, noise-canceling headphones can help keep the volume at a safe level.</p>

<p>Increasing your distance from the noise source can also make a significant difference. At concerts and sporting events, move away from speakers. If you’re at a loud event for several hours, step outside or find a quieter area periodically to give your ears a break. When using power tools, lawn equipment or other machinery, wear properly fitted earplugs or earmuffs from the start, rather than waiting until the noise becomes uncomfortable.</p>

<p>To help create a quieter environment at home, consider <a href="https://nymag.com/strategist/article/best-battery-powered-yard-tools.html">battery-powered lawn tools</a>, which are often quieter – and produce fewer emissions – than gas-powered models. When purchasing <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apacoust.2021.108099">household appliances such as dishwashers</a>, compare their noise ratings and choose quieter models when possible.</p>

<h2>Noise exposure is a public health problem</h2>

<p>Individual behaviors are important, but noise pollution won’t be solved one pair of earplugs at a time. Most people cannot control the noise they are exposed to. A farmer cannot turn down the noise on a tractor. A child cannot reroute the highway outside their bedroom. A restaurant employee may spend an entire shift around a live band and rowdy patrons, without the option to retreat to a quieter environment.</p>

<p>Although each of us can take steps to reduce the noise around us, individual actions only go so far without broader changes. Protecting public health also requires manufacturers to buy or design <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/prevent/eliminate.html">quieter equipment</a>, architects and builders to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s40726-023-00250-1">consider acoustics</a> in the design of buildings, city planners to reduce transportation noise and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s44213-022-00005-6">create quieter public spaces</a>, and employers to implement <a href="https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/guidelines/non-binding-guide-good-practice-application-directive-200310ec-noise-work">workplace controls</a> to reduce noise at its source.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290223/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Noise pollution is an occupational health hazard for many workers. urbazon/E+ via Getty Images The human body is remarkably good at getting used to the environment around it
You’ve probably experienced this if you’ve ever gone to a matinee and emerged from the dark theater into sunshine
Your eyes sting, so you squint and shield your face until they adjust to the bright sunlight
In the same way, the body can grow accustomed to constant noise
With repeated exposure to traffic, leaf blowers, construction, loud music, crowded restaurants, fitness classes and sporting events, you can become accustomed to loud environments
Over time, what once seemed unusually loud may barely register
But what feels normal isn’t necessarily safe
Noise is an important but often overlooked environmental health hazard, with effects ranging from hearing loss to cardiovascular disease
I think about noise constantly because I’m an audiologist and hearing scientist with expertise in occupational exposures
But hazardous noise isn’t limited to the workplace
You likely encounter noise every day without knowing when it poses a risk
The good news is that many of the harmful effects of noise are preventable – once you know what to listen for
Noise affects more than your ears The most obvious consequence of excessive noise is hearing damage
Loud sounds can damage delicate sensory cells in the inner ear, leading to permanent hearing loss
Tinnitus, or ringing in the ears , is another common consequence of noise exposure
But hearing damage is only part of the story
Chronic environmental noise can affect health through other pathways, too
Noise acts as a stressor , activating the autonomic nervous and endocrine systems and affecting heart rate, blood pressure and other physiological processes
It can also disturb sleep , triggering stress responses even without fully waking us
Over months or years, these repeated effects can take a toll on the body
Long-term traffic noise exposure has been linked to hypertension , coronary artery disease, stroke and Type 2 diabetes
Workplace noise recommendations are primarily designed to protect workers from hearing loss
In contrast, the World Health Organization’s environmental noise guidelines recommend lower levels because they consider longer exposure periods and broader effects on health
How loud is too loud? The risk from noise depends on how loud it is , how long you’re exposed and how close you are to the source
Extremely loud sounds, such as fireworks or gunshots, can damage hearing almost instantly , especially at close range
Other sounds, such as power tools, loud music or heavy traffic, can pose a risk more gradually , as exposure adds up over time
The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommends limiting occupational noise exposure to 85 A-weighted decibels, or dBA , averaged over an eight-hour workday
A-weighting adjusts the measurement to better reflect how the human ear responds to sound
For every 3 dBA increase, the recommended exposure time is cut in half

Similar benchmarks are used elsewhere: Australia limits workplace exposure to 85 dBA over 8 hours, while the European Union and Great Britain require protective measures beginning at 80 dBA and additional measures at 85 dBA, and both prohibit exposure above 87 dBA after accounting for hearing protection
Though regulatory details differ, 85 dBA averaged over eight hours is a widely used international benchmark for occupational noise
And you don’t get a fresh start each time you leave a noisy environment
Rather, noise exposure adds up over the course of a day
Spending four hours at 88 dBA uses the same maximum recommended daily noise dose as eight hours at 85 dBA
Time spent around loud traffic, using power tools, attending a sporting event or listening to loud music can all contribute to that daily dose
Over time, exposure to ambient noise from traffic or public transportation can cause long-term health problems

<title>As cities prepare for 2026’s super El Niño, some crucial blind spots can’t be ignored</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760311/original/file-20260916-50-x1bcrt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=42%2C456%2C2232%2C1488&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">An affordable-housing crisis and a growing homeless population led Los Angeles to declared a shelter crisis during the 2015-16 El Niño.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fernando-lopez-carries-possessions-along-the-los-angeles-news-photo/498136120?adppopup=true">David McNew/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>This year’s El Niño has the potential to be one of the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/weather/articles/c3ekg93vjz9o">strongest in living memory</a>, and the evidence is showing up around the world. </p>

<p>The U.S. just saw its <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/national-climate-202608">hottest summer on record</a> in the Lower 48 states. Drought is <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-el-nino-is-shaping-up-to-be-a-doozy-its-already-affecting-global-shipping-fish-behavior-and-heat-291490">slowing shipping in the Panama Canal</a>. The Pacific is experiencing an <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-second-hurricane-just-sideswiped-hawaii-why-the-islands-usual-force-field-seems-to-be-down-in-2026-291524">exceptionally busy hurricane season</a>, while the <a href="https://substack.com/home/post/p-215680819">Atlantic is unusually quiet</a>. Those are just a few early signs. Forecasters warn that this El Niño could bring <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/09/1168265">extreme heat, destructive storms and flooding</a> to many parts of the planet through early 2027. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Huge waves crash up against a coastline. Their spray goes as high as the homes that are right next to the water." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760312/original/file-20260916-50-pyt3pg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Storm waves crash onto seaside houses at Mondos Beach, Calif., on Jan. 12, 2016, during a strong El Niño.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/el-nino-generated-storm-waves-crash-onto-seaside-houses-at-news-photo/504713230?adppopup=true">Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I am a <a href="https://www.climatepolicylab.org/bethany-tietjen">researcher who works on climate and disaster resilience</a>, and I study how governments prepare for climate disasters and help to identify what they are missing.</p>

<p>Community planning for El Niño often starts by identifying infrastructure that’s vulnerable to extreme weather. What can be harder to address are the needs of the populations most at risk, including low-income communities and older adults who may need help preparing their homes and themselves for extreme conditions. </p>

<p>As communities prepare for the rising risk of extreme weather, they need to be aware of the blind spots.</p>

<h2>What is El Niño and what’s at risk?</h2>

<p>El Niño is part of a <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">natural climate pattern</a> that appears every few years when temperatures in the eastern Pacific Ocean rise.</p>

<p>Its effects can <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-el-nino-is-shaping-up-to-be-a-doozy-its-already-affecting-global-shipping-fish-behavior-and-heat-291490">shift weather patterns</a> away from what is considered normal. Typically wet regions can get unusually dry, while dry areas can experience extreme rainfall that causes flooding. Global average temperatures also tend to rise during El Niño conditions, leaving people facing <a href="https://theconversation.com/heat-waves-can-leave-homes-dangerously-hot-even-for-young-healthy-adults-272025">dangerous heat, both indoors</a> <a href="https://theconversation.com/extreme-heat-is-taking-a-toll-on-firefighters-as-wildfires-stretch-crews-to-the-limit-290571">and outdoors</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/WPA-KpldDVc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">What is El Niño?</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>On the U.S. West Coast, for example, the <a href="https://www.ppic.org/blog/supercharged-sea-levels-this-winter-will-forecast-the-future/">combination of El Niño conditions with king tides and rising sea levels</a> could lead to more coastal flooding, erosion and damage to homes and infrastructure. In the past, <a href="https://www.conservation.ca.gov/cgs/landslides/el-nino">flood damage and landslides</a> from heavy rain during El Niño have shut down highways and affected public services long after a storm has passed.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map of the US shows rainier conditions in the South, warmth in Canada and the northern U.S., and dryness in the Midwest." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760105/original/file-20260916-50-jzxivo.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In winter, El Niño typically shifts weather patterns across the U.S. However, every El Nino is different – conditions during one El Niño may be very different from the next.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters">NOAA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Preparing for the <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml">strong El Niño expected in late 2026</a> and early 2027 means ensuring that critical infrastructure is able to withstand flooding, temperature extremes and other severe weather conditions.</p>

<p>That means inspecting flood control and drainage systems, trimming trees that could knock down power lines during high winds, and reinforcing or maintaining infrastructure such as <a href="https://www.smdp.com/county-outlines-el-nino-storm-preparations-as-forecasters-warn-of-historic-season/">dams</a>, <a href="https://www.ci.oceanside.ca.us/Home/Components/News/News/1042/14?">stormwater channels</a>, <a href="https://www.sandiego.gov/elnino">roads and bridges</a>.</p>

<p>Aging infrastructure, in particular, can be a problem. </p>

<p><a href="https://infrastructurereportcard.org/cat-item/dams-infrastructure/">Old levees and dams</a>, for example, can leave a community vulnerable to catastrophic flooding, as the Seattle area saw in December 2025 when <a href="https://theconversation.com/west-coast-levee-failures-show-the-rising-risks-from-americas-aging-flood-defenses-272556">flooding from heavy rainfall broke levees</a> in multiple communities. Repairing and replacing large-scale infrastructure like this is expensive and time-consuming. Too often, by the time it fails, <a href="https://theconversation.com/heavy-rain-on-snow-is-testing-aging-dams-across-michigan-and-wisconsin-this-is-the-future-in-a-warming-world-281221">repairs had been discussed for years</a> but not completed.</p>

<h2>Where we’re finding gaps in disaster planning</h2>

<p>Infrastructure is only part of the challenge. Preparing a community for El Niño also means preparing people for what could be unprecedented conditions.</p>

<p>A study I worked on with researchers at Tufts University reviewed climate adaptation and disaster preparedness in several high-risk communities in the United States. We <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2024.102882">identified gaps</a> in the policies, resources and institutional capacity available to help communities adapt to rising risks.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A paved bicycling path atop a levee is broken and slabs of asphalt pavement are tilted into a breach where water poured through." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/710344/original/file-20251225-56-c5qsog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Crews inspect damage to a Green River levee in the Seattle suburbs on Dec. 15, 2025. Thousands of people were urged to evacuate during a series of atmospheric river storms, and the National Guard was sent to monitor and reinforce several levees considered at risk.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/ExtremeWeatherWashington/d6e74ec36c664ee88b4a43c6abb0b7c5/photo">AP Photo/Manuel Valdes</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In particular, we found that governments often focus heavily on physical risks while giving too little attention to <a href="https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/111729">social vulnerability</a>.</p>

<p>Vulnerable populations, including people experiencing homelessness, older adults and people with disabilities, often face <a href="https://theconversation.com/evacuating-in-disasters-like-hurricane-milton-isnt-simple-there-are-reasons-people-stay-in-harms-way-240869">higher risks and greater challenges in preparing for disasters</a>. </p>

<p>People with limited mobility, for example, may have <a href="https://www.ready.gov/people-disabilities">difficulty evacuating quickly or getting into shelters</a>. Individuals with limited financial resources might have <a href="https://www.povertylaw.org/article/what-natural-disasters-reveal-about-racism-and-poverty-2/">fewer options for relocating or for making home improvements</a> in preparation for extreme weather. Someone experiencing homelessness may not have safe shelter.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man walks carefully through water as two mattress float away in a rush of water under a bridge." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760106/original/file-20260916-60-x6qjfq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In the Los Angeles area, homeless people often set up camp in normally dry riverbeds. But those areas are at high risk of flooding during El Niño. Heavy rains during the 2015-16 El Niño swept away this camp’s mattresses.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/felipe-flores-lopez-bed-floats-away-as-he-looses-his-news-photo/503500210?adppopup=true">Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>It is often easier for governments to identify and invest in physical infrastructure than to invest in policies that address complex social vulnerabilities like these. For example, building a seawall can be <a href="https://www.nlc.org/article/2026/07/16/where-do-cities-get-most-infrastructure-funding-municipal-bonds/">tied to a specific project or funding stream</a>. Reducing social vulnerability, on the other hand, may require coordination across housing, healthcare, emergency management and social services. And it typically requires sustained investments over time. </p>

<p>Yet, preparing successfully for extreme weather often requires considering housing and shelter needs, healthcare access and support services. </p>

<p>After a wildfire or major flooding, people may need <a href="https://theconversation.com/rents-rise-faster-after-disasters-but-a-federal-program-can-help-restrain-excesses-247307">temporary rental assistance or affordable housing</a> to avoid displacement. Older adults or people with disabilities may need <a href="https://theconversation.com/evacuating-in-disasters-like-hurricane-milton-isnt-simple-there-are-reasons-people-stay-in-harms-way-240869">transportation to shelters or assistance</a> getting medications and healthcare. </p>



<p>Many of these needs <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2024.102882">can be difficult to address</a> because the underlying vulnerabilities are deeply entrenched. Issues such as <a href="https://apnews.com/article/affordable-housing-shortage-poorest-us-80fab2a0fb645e4d629b0ef7e3c2b496">affordable housing shortages</a>, poverty or difficulty accessing healthcare cannot be solved by a single disaster-preparedness policy. But they do <a href="https://theconversation.com/in-many-of-appalachias-flood-ravaged-areas-residents-have-little-choice-but-rebuild-in-risky-locations-240429">shape how communities are able to recover</a> from extreme weather. </p>

<h2>Identifying gaps before extreme weather strikes</h2>

<p>A community’s preparedness often improves after an event, when the gaps become obvious. The challenge is identifying those gaps before a disaster occurs.</p>

<p>In Los Angeles, emergency managers are using a good method to meet that challenge in 2026: They are carrying out <a href="https://laist.com/news/climate-environment/la-county-emergency-managers-rush-to-prepare-for-el-nino">scenario exercises</a> that bring together county departments and community disaster management coordinators to practice how they would respond to an El-Niño-driven extreme weather event. </p>

<p>These exercises are designed to identify gaps in existing plans and figure out what might be needed if severe storms, flooding or mudslides occur. <a href="https://www.planning.org/knowledgebase/scenarioplanning/">Scenario exercises</a> allow people involved in disaster response to work through a hypothetical event before it happens. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several vehicles are tipped and trapped in mud up their windows along a highway." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=388&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=388&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=388&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=488&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=488&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760313/original/file-20260916-50-a3p91o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=488&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Heavy downpours in October 2015 caused mudslides that trapped vehicles on Interstate 5 north of Los Angeles. The storm was early in the season for El Niño damage and served as a warning of the risks to come.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/police-cars-drive-past-vehicles-that-are-stuck-on-a-road-news-photo/493001850">Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In both the <a href="https://www.kqed.org/news/12097546/el-nino-could-bring-a-wet-wild-winter-how-can-you-and-your-home-be-ready">San Francisco Bay Area</a> and in <a href="https://dconc.gov/Engineering-and-Environmental1/Documents/Sustainability/July-August-2026-Durham-County-Sustainability-Blog.pdf">Durham County, North Carolina</a>, officials are talking publicly about the risks to encourage residents to prepare. Bay Area officials are stressing the importance of following emergency management notifications and weather forecasts, particularly for individuals living close to the water or on hillsides that could face flash flooding and landslides.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://www.ci.oceanside.ca.us/Home/Components/News/News/1042/">Oceanside, California</a>, city officials convened an El Niño working group that included representatives from their public works, engineering, fire and police departments to coordinate planning, communications strategies and the monitoring of the San Luis Rey River.</p>

<h2>Broader lessons</h2>

<p>The challenge of preparing for El Niño in the face of uncertainty reflects some of the broader issues humanity faces when preparing for <a href="https://theconversation.com/climate-change-is-intensifying-the-water-cycle-bringing-more-powerful-storms-and-flooding-heres-what-the-science-shows-187951">future climate changes</a>.</p>

<p>Keeping up with infrastructure maintenance, scenario planning ahead of heat or storm seasons, understanding the needs of vulnerable populations and having plans in place to meet them can help prevent a severe storm from becoming a major disaster for the community.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290787/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

What is El Niño and what’s at risk? El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that appears every few years when temperatures in the eastern Pacific Ocean rise
Its effects can shift weather patterns away from what is considered normal
Typically wet regions can get unusually dry, while dry areas can experience extreme rainfall that causes flooding
Global average temperatures also tend to rise during El Niño conditions, leaving people facing dangerous heat, both indoors and outdoors
West Coast, for example, the combination of El Niño conditions with king tides and rising sea levels could lead to more coastal flooding, erosion and damage to homes and infrastructure

<title>How employers can make good decisions about remote work before the next crisis strikes</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760274/original/file-20260916-60-3tfj7q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C74%2C4847%2C3231&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, many employers ended up with hybrid work arrangements.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/cambridge-ma-some-employees-back-at-work-in-the-kayak-news-photo/1236663903?adppopup=true">David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>More than six years after the COVID-19 pandemic began, <a href="https://www.minneapolisfed.org/article/2026/is-remote-work-declining-what-the-latest-data-show">over 1 in 5</a> of the U.S. workers who can work remotely do so either full time or at least one day per week.</p>

<p>Even though a new normal has set in, no single approach has worked for all employees. And the debate over the <a href="https://time.com/partner-content/charter/why-you-shouldn-t-let-ceos-nostalgia-drive-remote-work/">benefits and drawbacks of remote work</a> continues. </p>

<p>To see what factors affected the long-term shift to remote and hybrid work that kept going after the pandemic subsided, and to learn more about the pandemic’s effects on research firms more broadly, <a href="https://www.babson.edu/about/our-leaders-and-scholars/faculty-and-academic-divisions/faculty-profiles/sebastian-fixson.php">I teamed up with my Babson College colleagues</a>, <a href="https://www.babson.edu/about/our-leaders-and-scholars/faculty-and-academic-divisions/faculty-profiles/gina-oconnor.php">Gina O’Connor</a> and <a href="https://www.babson.edu/about/our-leaders-and-scholars/faculty-and-academic-divisions/faculty-profiles/jonathan-sims.php">Jonathan Sims</a>.</p>

<p>We found that the process used to decide where employees should work <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08956308.2026.2697696">matters just as much as the decision itself</a>.</p>



<h2>Facing the same challenge</h2>

<p>In early 2020, the research and development units of four global companies were conducting similar technical and scientific work. They all had access to the same communication technologies when COVID-19 upended everyone’s routine. </p>

<p>In keeping with social science research methods, we agreed to not name any of these companies. As we learned through a series of interviews with senior leaders, project team leaders and team members from 2021 to 2023, all four companies told most of their employees to work from home in March 2020.</p>

<p>What unfolded over the next three years in terms of how they arranged how and where employees would work as waves of COVID-19 came and went – remote, on-site or hybrid – differed in terms of the time it took them to arrive at stable work arrangements and the degree to which workers agreed with them.</p>

<p>Other research into how likely an employer is to allow remote and hybrid work arrangements after the pandemic has focused on executives’ traits, <a href="http://www.nber.org/papers/w34795">such as their age</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2026.104496">personalities</a>. But we’ve found that these choices regarding where employees work can have more to do with an employer’s <a href="https://www.elgaronline.com/edcollbook/edcoll/9781788976251/9781788976251.xml">organizational culture</a>: the set of assumptions, beliefs and norms that shape how people who work together make decisions and interact with each other.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man works at an otherwise empty and large office." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=404&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=404&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=404&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=508&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=508&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760275/original/file-20260916-60-air5gg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=508&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Drew Allison, a Fuze executive, works at his office in Boston on March 10, 2020, as millions of Americans begin to work from home amid coronavirus concerns.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/drew-allison-world-wide-brand-creative-director-at-fuze-news-photo/1206475720?adppopup=true">David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Attaining stable work arrangements</h2>

<p>A Stanford University research team found in another study published in 2026 that the <a href="https://wfhresearch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/WFHResearch_updates_September2026.pdf">average percentage of paid full days worked from home</a> shot from 7% shortly before the pandemic began to more than 60% soon after it started; the share of days spent working remotely then declined over the next two years to roughly 30%.</p>

<p>We noticed significant variations from this pattern among the four companies we studied. </p>

<p>For most scientists and technicians, fully remote work lasted between a few weeks and a few months. For the four companies we studied, it took 3-15 months to establish new stable work arrangements, sometimes with multiple workplace policy changes along the way.</p>

<p>Second, managers and employees understood, agreed with and accepted new work arrangements to very different degrees.</p>

<p>By early 2023, middle managers and workers at two of the four employers broadly accepted their companies’ work-from-home policies. At one of the other two, workers generally accepted it; at the other one, employees rejected the policies and were finding work-arounds to policies they disagreed with.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman works from home while her cat saunters toward her." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760281/original/file-20260916-50-pr4k7f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">DrFirst employee Heather Happe sits at her desk next to her cat Duncan at her home in Frederick, Md., on Jan. 14, 2025. Her company went fully remote during the pandemic and stayed that way once it ended.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/drfirsts-employee-heather-happe-sits-at-her-desk-next-to-news-photo/2194058980?adppopup=true">Agnes Bun/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Being hierarchical or collaborative</h2>

<p>Because it develops slowly over years, organizational culture is hard to change. When a crisis strikes, that culture acts like a script that determines which decisions feel possible and which seem untenable.</p>

<p>We found that organizational culture determined how quickly an employer succeeded at establishing a new balance between remote, on-site and hybrid work after the earliest phase of the pandemic had passed.</p>

<p>Two of the employers established procedures and enforced clear lines of authority and rules regarding when employees could work from home. A research director at one of these highly hierarchical companies described the pandemic as “just another risk that needed to be managed” using existing protocols. These employers stabilized work arrangements quickly, and employees understood “the rules.”</p>

<p>The other two emphasized teamwork and participation, welcoming employee input in decisions. One of the two companies with collaborative cultures held workshops about the use of remote work, which included employees at every level – ensuring that all employees would understand what was being done and why. </p>

<p>Both kinds of cultures had strengths and weaknesses during and after the pandemic.</p>

<p>The hierarchical companies moved faster but struggled more with managerial issues over workplace policies when many of their employees felt their concerns were not heard. In contrast, the collaborative companies took longer to decide on their workplace policies but encountered less pushback from their employees.</p>

<p>Organizational culture can shape and limit an employer’s decisions during a crisis.  Because developing a culture that is more flexible takes time, we believe employers should consider getting started on that process long before the next crisis hits and disrupts many work routines.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/282671/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images More than six years after the COVID-19 pandemic began, over 1 in 5 of the U.S. workers who can work remotely do so either full time or at least one day per week
Even though a new normal has set in, no single approach has worked for all employees
And the debate over the benefits and drawbacks of remote work continues

To see what factors affected the long-term shift to remote and hybrid work that kept going after the pandemic subsided, and to learn more about the pandemic’s effects on research firms more broadly, I teamed up with my Babson College colleagues , Gina O’Connor and Jonathan Sims
We found that the process used to decide where employees should work matters just as much as the decision itself
Facing the same challenge In early 2020, the research and development units of four global companies were conducting similar technical and scientific work
They all had access to the same communication technologies when COVID-19 upended everyone’s routine
In keeping with social science research methods, we agreed to not name any of these companies

As we learned through a series of interviews with senior leaders, project team leaders and team members from 2021 to 2023, all four companies told most of their employees to work from home in March 2020

What unfolded over the next three years in terms of how they arranged how and where employees would work as waves of COVID-19 came and went – remote, on-site or hybrid – differed in terms of the time it took them to arrive at stable work arrangements and the degree to which workers agreed with them
Other research into how likely an employer is to allow remote and hybrid work arrangements after the pandemic has focused on executives’ traits, such as their age and personalities

But we’ve found that these choices regarding where employees work can have more to do with an employer’s organizational culture : the set of assumptions, beliefs and norms that shape how people who work together make decisions and interact with each other
Drew Allison, a Fuze executive, works at his office in Boston on March 10, 2020, as millions of Americans begin to work from home amid coronavirus concerns

Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Attaining stable work arrangements A Stanford University research team found in another study published in 2026 that the average percentage of paid full days worked from home shot from 7% shortly before the pandemic began to more than 60% soon after it started; the share of days spent working remotely then declined over the next two years to roughly 30%
We noticed significant variations from this pattern among the four companies we studied
For most scientists and technicians, fully remote work lasted between a few weeks and a few months
For the four companies we studied, it took 3-15 months to establish new stable work arrangements, sometimes with multiple workplace policy changes along the way
Second, managers and employees understood, agreed with and accepted new work arrangements to very different degrees
By early 2023, middle managers and workers at two of the four employers broadly accepted their companies’ work-from-home policies
At one of the other two, workers generally accepted it; at the other one, employees rejected the policies and were finding work-arounds to policies they disagreed with
DrFirst employee Heather Happe sits at her desk next to her cat Duncan at her home in Frederick, Md., on Jan. 14, 2025
Her company went fully remote during the pandemic and stayed that way once it ended
Agnes Bun/AFP via Getty Images Being hierarchical or collaborative Because it develops slowly over years, organizational culture is hard to change
When a crisis strikes, that culture acts like a script that determines which decisions feel possible and which seem untenable

We found that organizational culture determined how quickly an employer succeeded at establishing a new balance between remote, on-site and hybrid work after the earliest phase of the pandemic had passed
Two of the employers established procedures and enforced clear lines of authority and rules regarding when employees could work from home
A research director at one of these highly hierarchical companies described the pandemic as “just another risk that needed to be managed” using existing protocols
These employers stabilized work arrangements quickly, and employees understood “the rules.” The other two emphasized teamwork and participation, welcoming employee input in decisions

One of the two companies with collaborative cultures held workshops about the use of remote work, which included employees at every level – ensuring that all employees would understand what was being done and why
Both kinds of cultures had strengths and weaknesses during and after the pandemic
The hierarchical companies moved faster but struggled more with managerial issues over workplace policies when many of their employees felt their concerns were not heard
In contrast, the collaborative companies took longer to decide on their workplace policies but encountered less pushback from their employees
Organizational culture can shape and limit an employer’s decisions during a crisis
Because developing a culture that is more flexible takes time, we believe employers should consider getting started on that process long before the next crisis hits and disrupts many work routines
The research team received funding from the Innovation Research Interchange for transcription services.

title: The higher your body fat percentage, the less accurate your smartwatch is at measuring calories you burn when exercising – new study
