<title>The higher your body fat percentage, the less accurate your smartwatch is at measuring calories you burn when exercising – new study</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760324/original/file-20260916-50-1qj6ua.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5504&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Study participants rode a recumbent bike while wearing four smartwatches and breathing into a metabolic analyzer.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Taimy Alvarez/Florida International University</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>Smartwatches have become an increasingly popular way for people to monitor their health and fitness. About 100 million – <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/06/17/americans-and-ai-2026-chatbots-smart-devices-and-views-on-impact/">nearly 4 in 10 – U.S. adults</a> own a smartwatch. Worldwide, market research estimates <a href="https://www.demandsage.com/smartwatch-statistics/">approximately 560 million smartwatch wearers</a>.</p>

<p>Yet a <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/s26082526">growing body of research</a> demonstrates that one of the most commonly used smartwatch metrics – number of calories burned – is often inaccurate.</p>

<p>I’m an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JVhRD30AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">exercise scientist</a>, and I study physical activity behavior and the integration of wearable technology. I recently worked with a team of colleagues at <a href="https://web.eng.fiu.edu/jramella/">Florida International University’s Medical Photonics Laboratory</a> on a study examining <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353261">how well commonly used smartwatches measure physiological responses</a> during exercise, and whether that accuracy differs across individuals.</p>

<p>Our team found that not only can these devices err substantially in their measurements of calories burned, but those errors also increase as the wearer’s body fat percentage rises.</p>

<h2>Smartwatch basics</h2>

<p>Most <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/accelerometer">smartwatches contain accelerometers</a> that measure movement and use a light-based sensor to estimate heart rate. With each heartbeat, the amount of blood flowing through the vessels in your wrist changes. Blood absorbs light, allowing the watch to track changes in the light reflected back to the sensor. That pattern allows the watch to estimate your heart rate.</p>

<p>The watch combines the data from these sensors with information about the user, such as age, sex, height and weight. It then uses an algorithm to estimate how much energy that person expended.</p>

<p>Heart rate and movement are relatively accessible signals for a wrist-worn device, but caloric expenditure is much more complex. It requires the watch to use several pieces of information that it can measure reasonably well to predict something it cannot measure directly. But differences in the wearers’ body composition, fitness, movement efficiency and physiological responses to exercise can all affect that prediction.</p>

<h2>How we did the study</h2>

<p>For our study, we recruited 58 Hispanic adults from Miami, where our lab is located, representing a wide range of body fat percentages and skin tones. These differences allowed us to ask not only whether the watches were accurate overall, but whether their accuracy changed <a href="https://doi.org/10.1364/BOE.439893">depending on who was wearing them</a>.</p>

<p>Each participant completed a standardized cycling session while wearing four popular consumer devices: an Apple Watch Series 8, Garmin Forerunner 955, Samsung Galaxy Watch5 and Fitbit Sense 2. Participants alternated between moderate- and vigorous-intensity exercise on a recumbent bicycle for 10 minutes. </p>

<p>As they pedaled, we measured their energy expenditure using a metabolic analyzer, which captures and measures the gases a person inhales and exhales via a mask. In exercise science, this is considered the most reliable way to measure calorie expenditure. That measurement gave us a value against which we could compare each watch’s calorie estimate.</p>

<p>Our protocol provided the watches with a relatively controlled environment in which to perform. We intentionally used recumbent cycling because it allowed us to tightly control exercise intensity while reducing wrist movement, which can interfere with the heart rate measurement used by wearable devices. </p>

<p>Each participant wore two watches on each wrist. We randomized their placements just in case one position provided an advantage. We didn’t find any evidence it did.</p>

<p><iframe id="rONrz" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rONrz/4/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Four lines showing predicted difference between the estimated number of calories from each brand of smartwatches and the actual calories burned, across body fat percentage."></iframe></p>

<h2>Substantial error</h2>

<p>All four watches demonstrated substantial error in measuring caloric expenditure. The median error across the devices was about 15% to 25%, meaning that even before considering individual differences, the watches’ estimates were often meaningfully different from our laboratory measurement.</p>

<p>Apple, Garmin and Samsung all systematically overestimated caloric expenditure. Apple had the smallest average systematic error, while Garmin and Samsung produced larger overestimates.</p>

<p>Fitbit presented a different problem. Although its average error was not systematically positive or negative after data-quality exclusions, it produced several clearly implausible estimates, which we treated as device errors, including seven readings exceeding 450% of the value measured by the metabolic system.</p>

<p>The general inaccuracy was not particularly surprising and has been <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/s26082526">well-documented in previous research</a>. What surprised us was the strength of the relationship between body fat percentage and error. We found that as body fat percentage went up – meaning the more body fat the wearer had – the more inaccurate the watch’s measurements of calories burned. </p>

<p>This was true for all the devices we tested, although the magnitude of the effect varied significantly by brand. The errors for some watches ranged from about 50% to 100% or even more for the study participants with higher body fat percentages.</p>

<p>To put that into more practical terms, imagine that our gold-standard metabolic analyzer measured an energy expenditure of 100 calories during an exercise session. A 50% overestimate would result in the watch displaying approximately 150 calories. A 100% overestimate would result in the watch displaying approximately 200 calories.</p>

<p>We did not find that skin tone had a significant effect on caloric expenditure error under the conditions we tested.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a person wearing four different brands of smartwatch, two on each wrist" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760325/original/file-20260916-50-n5t4s4.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">All four of the smartwatch brands tested showed substantial errors in measuring calorie expenditure.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Taimy Alvarez/Florida International University</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What this means for smartwatch users</h2>

<p>We cannot determine from this study why body fat percentage had such a substantial effect. How the estimation algorithms are developed and calibrated may also play an important role, but because each device uses its own version of a proprietary algorithm, we can’t know exactly how it is measuring caloric expenditure.</p>

<p>People with higher body fat percentages are likely among those most interested in using wearable devices to support weight loss. Yet our results indicate that they may also receive the least accurate estimates of caloric expenditure.</p>

<p>An error of 50 or 100 calories in a single short exercise session may not seem particularly important, but that error can add up over time. In practical terms, if you have a body fat content of 35% or more and you’re exercising 4 hours a week, your watch could be 1,200-2,400 calories off per week. If you’re trying to manage your weight using your watch’s output, you could be consuming nearly an entire day’s worth of calories in error, thinking you’d burned them in your workouts during the week.</p>

<h2>What consumers can do</h2>

<p>This does not mean smartwatches have no value.</p>

<p>In a companion study using the same exercise protocol, our team found that these devices <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/s26102922">measure heart rate with reasonable accuracy</a>. Depending on the activity, these devices can also provide useful information about other metrics, including workout duration, distance and pace.</p>

<p>Based on the results of our study, I recommend that smartwatch users treat the calorie number as an estimate rather than an exact measurement. If your goal is to lose weight, I would be conservative about using that number to determine how much to eat or to evaluate the success of a workout.</p>

<p>Looking at patterns over time may also be useful, particularly when considered alongside heart rate, exercise intensity, changes in body weight and your own experience. However, a consistent number is not necessarily an accurate number. A device can systematically overestimate caloric expenditure and still appear very consistent from workout to workout.</p>

<p>Wearable technology will continue to improve. Better sensors may contribute to that progress, but improving how energy expenditure is estimated across people with different body compositions may be just as important.</p>

<p>In our lab, we are now extending our experiments with smartwatches to strength training, where the combination of wrist and whole-body movement, along with varying exercise intensity, may make accurate estimation even more challenging. Other labs around the world are also working to improve these technologies and learn how they can better inform health decisions.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291632/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Scientists are finally starting to figure out Alzheimer’s
excerpt: A scan of the brain of a patient affected by Alzheimer's disease. | BSIP/UIG Via Getty Images For decades, research into Alzheimer’s disease has made painfully
body: A scan of the brain of a patient affected by Alzheimer's disease. | BSIP/UIG Via Getty Images For decades, research into Alzheimer’s disease has made painfully little progress
More than 7 million Americans are living with the disease, which is the most common cause of dementia
It’s incurable, and treatments have been hampered by groupthink, as well as by systemic fraud from some of the field’s most famous researchers

But there are finally signs that the field is turning a corner, including two new drugs , rolled out in the last few years, that can treat Alzheimer’s directly. “If somebody walks into a clinic right now and is diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease,” Vox senior correspondent Dylan Scott tells Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram, the drugs “will hopefully have some effect in slowing down their cognitive decline.”  As Scott says, “The drug development pipeline is also starting to look much more robust” — even “revolutionary,” to quote one doctor he spoke with

The two talk about why researchers are more optimistic than they have been in years, whether GLP-1 drugs might help prevent Alzheimer’s, and an experimental surgery pioneered by doctors in China that has produced striking — but if unproven — reports of improvement in people with the disease
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Tell us what they are, Dylan? We have two drugs right now that have been approved by the FDA: lecanemab and donanemab
And these are drugs that target the amyloid plaque in the brain that scientists have long thought might be associated with the development of Alzheimer’s disease

The amyloid hypothesis [the belief that Alzheimer’s is caused by the buildup of deleterious amyloid proteins in the brain] has been very controversial for a while, in part because there were these years and years where we weren’t seeing any progress despite this being the dominant hypothesis about the disease
But we do have these two drugs that in clinical trials have been shown to both clear out the amyloid plaque in somebody’s brain and they do seem to lead to slower cognitive decline for those patients
And the hope is that this is the ground floor

These are the worst drugs, hopefully, that we’re ever going to have and continued scientific discovery and progress with developing drugs will lead to even better treatments in the future. “The hope is that five, 10 years from now, we’ve got a much more robust suite of treatments that can help somebody who’s been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s.” Tell us more about the scientific discovery

You mentioned that there’s promising research beyond amyloid plaques? It’s not like the amyloid hypothesis has been invalidated, but I think our understanding of the disease has become more complex.  We’re realizing that there’s probably also a role for a different kind of protein called tau
There may also be a role with chronic inflammation, your vascular health, your body’s ability to just pump blood through your body may also be playing a role in the development of Alzheimer’s disease

And so now we’re starting to see treatments that target these other things.  The way I’ve been thinking about it is if we used to be putting all of our bets on amyloid, we’re still putting some bets on amyloid, but we’re also putting bets on these other things
And so now there are treatments in the works targeting, for example, these tau proteins

They’re still in the early stages of clinical trials — really at the stage where they’re just checking the safety of these drugs and making sure that somebody can take them without getting really sick, or God forbid, dying or something like that

But even when they’re doing those safety checks, they do start to collect qualitative data about, well, are we starting to see any effects? Some of the preliminary results from some of these tau targeting treatments that are in the works have looked pretty promising
And so that’s encouraging, obviously

It’s possible that we’re moving towards a future where not unlike cancer treatment, there’s not just one drug for Alzheimer’s disease, but maybe you take a combination of different things that work on different mechanisms for the disease and the collective cumulative effect is that it stops the progression or even reverses it.  The hope is that five, 10 years from now, we’ve got a much more robust suite of treatments that can help somebody who’s been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s

Five, 10 years from now sounds nice, but is there anything else that’s in the cocktail now that people are discovering could be promising for Alzheimer’s? There are also, yes, drugs that millions of people are taking right now for other reasons that might also be able to help with Alzheimer’s disease
And GLP-1s in particular are the big ones
These drugs — it seems like every day you see some new headline about this miraculous thing that they can do
Weight loss, smoking, my poker addiction, and…? And it might prevent dementia down the road.  If you step back and think about it, the theory does make some sense
Like I said before, scientists increasingly think there’s an association between your vascular health and your cognitive health, especially as you age

And what do these GLP-1 drugs do? They help people lose weight.  Losing weight helps to lower your blood pressure, lowers your risk of vascular problems, whether it’s heart disease or pulmonary disease or stroke or something like that

So if more and more people take these, they take them earlier in life, they lose weight, they keep it off, they don’t develop these heart or vascular problems, it does make some sense that that may also reduce their risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.  It’s still sort of theoretical, but the Alzheimer’s Association is putting $100 million behind some research projects to investigate this possible link
We may learn five, 10 years from now, as millions of people are now on these GLP-1 drugs — maybe we start to see Alzheimer’s less often
And that would be another reason to be optimistic that the future for this disease is looking brighter
How about reversing it? Is that still a pie in the sky? It’s out of reach for now
Certainly some of the scientists that I’ve talked to have said, “In theory, it should be possible

It’s really good at rebuilding itself if you give it the chance.” It seems like it should be possible to stop the progression of the disease eventually, and maybe ultimately reverse it.  Now, there has been some really intriguing, but also mysterious developments around reversing Alzheimer’s, not from scientists based out of the United States, but from scientists in China
People may or may not have seen that there have been videos of these patients who underwent an experimental surgery and the before and after of these videos is incredible
In the before, you’ve got somebody who clearly has Alzheimer’s disease, doesn’t recognize their loved ones, has trouble with their train of thought
In the after videos, it’s like they’re a completely different person
They recognize their loved ones, they’re talking articulately
And so that has, as you can imagine, generated a lot of excitement, also a fair bit of skepticism
Are these videos real? Do we know? We don’t know for sure if they’re real or not

What’s intriguing about this surgery is that the theory of it, at least to me as a lay person, makes some sense.  The gist of this surgery is the surgeons create a drain in the patient’s brain and the drain is supposed to help the brain get rid of these amyloid and tau proteins that we think are associated with Alzheimer’s disease

title: The United Nations looks broken. Is it?
excerpt: Law enforcement officers outside the United Nations headquarters ahead of the UN General Assembly on September 21, 2026. | Angelina Katsanis/Bloomberg via Getty
body: Law enforcement officers outside the United Nations headquarters ahead of the UN General Assembly on September 21, 2026. | Angelina Katsanis/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

It’s time for yet another United Nations General Assembly meeting in Manhattan — just one year after President Donald Trump appeared at it and asked,  bluntly : “What is the purpose of the United Nations?” Every year around this time, roughly 130 leaders from around the world convene at the UN to deliver speeches, hold diplomatic meetings, and debate issues like AI, climate change, and the wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran

Trump is scheduled to speak this week, as are Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (…despite New York’s chilly reception ).  Even more important than those big public speeches, however, are the one-on-one talks between foreign leaders
Trump has a packed meeting schedule on Monday and Tuesday, featuring the likes of Zelenskyy, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham
In Trump’s famously bizarre speech last year, he attacked several US allies, called climate change a “con,” and  suggested the UN itself was irrelevant
Increasingly — as we’ll get into below — that’s an accusation echoed by many UN critics

Go a little deeper View Link This week’s meeting comes at a moment of crisis — or at the very least, inflection — for the United Nations.  The UN faces a severe budgetary shortfall this year, caused largely by Trump’s refusal to pay America’s full dues

At the same time, the UN has battled searing criticism of its inability to end conflicts in places like Ukraine, Iran, and Gaza.  Under the organization’s founding charter, any of the five permanent members of its Security Council — the body responsible for maintaining international security — can block important resolutions unilaterally
In 2022, Russia controversially used that power to torpedo a resolution condemning its attempted annexation of parts of Ukraine
Three years later, the US similarly vetoed a demand for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza and an increase in unrestricted humanitarian aid
Critics point to impasses like these as evidence the UN no longer works; even UN Secretary-General António Guterres has said the Security Council needs reform

But it would be a mistake to conclude the UN is somehow irrelevant or newly ineffectual.  For one thing, Security Council gridlock isn’t a recent development — it’s the historical norm . (Check out all the Cold War-era vetoes in the chart above.) The UN is also far more than its Security Council — it’s a sprawling humanitarian apparatus that provides food, cash aid, medical care, and other assistance to millions around the world.  In Gaza last year alone, for instance, the UN says it provided clean water to 1.6 million people, operated dozens of makeshift schools for Palestinian children, and distributed almost $55 million of humanitarian cash assistance
Those efforts probably won’t make headlines this week
But they help answer Trump’s 2025 question
One link for later ➨ Put yourself first for once
A striking new poll finds that healthcare challenges prevent a sizable plurality of women from having the careers, social relationships, and family lives they want
The problem is overwhelmingly structural, of course

But in an exclusive interview with Vox , the philanthropist Melinda French Gates warns that women are also “often taught to put themselves last,” especially when they’re caregivers.   Before you go… Did you know …that crows can solve puzzles as well as 5-year-olds? In one study, they were observed bending a piece of wire to fish a treat out of a tube

Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the US Supreme Court justice who succeeded John Paul Stevens
That would be Elena Kagan, an Obama nominee who was confirmed to the court in 2010.

title: Obsessing about being a good person can backfire. There’s a better way.
excerpt: Editor’s note, September 20, 8 am ET:  We’re bringing you some of our best-loved  Your Mileage May Vary  columns while Sigal Samuel is on parenta
body: Editor’s note, September 20, 8 am ET:  We’re bringing you some of our best-loved  Your Mileage May Vary  columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave
The one below was originally published last September
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
The Jewish High Holidays are coming up, and that includes Yom Kippur
It’s a holiday that encourages people to reflect on their behavior and make amends
That’s all well and good, but I’m someone who struggles with scrupulosity — constantly worrying about my morality and if I’m doing The Most Possible Good ™
In practice this is far more paralyzing than motivating

Fixating on the ethical implications of all possible decisions makes it harder to take any action, and I’ve lost hours scouring my memories of my past behavior for immorality like a football player watching footage of their games to analyze what they could do differently
Guilt simply isn’t serving me, but I worry that saying to hell with all that means I’ll stop striving to be a better person and become morally complacent
I’ve observed Yom Kippur for decades, and don’t want to simply avoid the day
But the holiday is a moral scrupulosity trigger
How do you think I should approach this? I want to stop feeling guilty for letting guilt get in my own way
Dear Scrupulous,  Have you ever heard the story about what happened when God decided to give the Bible to flesh-and-blood human beings? According to the ancient rabbis, the angels hated the idea

They argued that humans were deeply flawed mortals who didn’t deserve such a holy scripture; only angels could be worthy of it, so it should stay up in heaven.  It fell to Moses to rebut the angels’ argument

He asked them: What do you angels need the Bible for? The Bible says not to murder, not to commit adultery, not to steal — do you have jealousy or other emotions that could lead you to do those things? The Bible says to honor your father and mother — but you don’t have parents, so how could you ever do that? And the Bible says to sanctify the Sabbath — but you never do any work, so how could you even honor the Sabbath by resting?  The angels saw that Moses was right
Angels are really great at one thing: being perfect
They don’t experience painful challenges, they don’t grow, and they don’t make choices that add beauty to the world

God gives the Bible to humans not to make them into angels — but to make them better at being the unique thing they are: human animals, with feelings, flaws, and all, that can learn to use their capabilities in more beautiful ways

Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! I think there’s a lot of wisdom in this story

And I want you to notice how far it is from demanding that humans do “The Most Possible Good™.” That language suggests a maximizing ethical theory like utilitarianism, which says that we have to do the action that produces the greatest good for the greatest number
In other words, we have to optimize.  Moral optimization may be possible for angels, but not for humans
We each hold multiple values, and sometimes those values are in tension with each other, forcing us to strike a balance as best we can
We’re not omniscient beings who can know with certainty how best to strike the balance.  What’s more, sometimes different kinds of moral good straight-up conflict with each other
Think of a woman who faces a trade-off: She wants to become a nun but also wants to become a mother
She can’t balance between those options — she has to choose
And what’s the better choice? We can’t say because the options are incommensurable
There’s no single yardstick by which to measure them so we can’t compare them to find out which is greater
Given that this complexity is baked into the human condition, it’s impossible to be a perfect optimizing machine
And the more you try to force yourself to be that, the harder it’ll be for you to actually help others, because you’ll just be so burned out
As you’ve already discovered, the optimizing mindset is exhausting — you end up expending a lot of precious mental resources that you could be spending on something else
And a lot of the time, there’s no knowably best decision
So instead of trying to optimize everything, you can adopt a goal that’s humbler but more realistic: to live in line with your values as best you can.  I know that can feel scary
Optimizing makes being human feel less risky
It provides a sense of control, and therefore a sense of safety
The unspoken premise is that if you optimize, you’ll never have to ask yourself: How could I screw up that badly?  But there’s another way to feel safe
It’s about leaning into the fact that we are imperfect and vulnerable creatures and that even when we’re trying our hardest there will be some things that we do not do optimally
Of course, we should still try to live in line with our values

But in those moments when we fall short, we shouldn’t berate ourselves, thinking, “I sinned!” In Hebrew, the word we typically translate as “to sin” (lachto) actually means “to miss the mark.” It’s the same word we’d use to describe someone with a bow and arrow who’s targeting the bullseye but misses it slightly

title: Why we should all be partying more
excerpt: We are in the midst of a loneliness epidemic: More than half of Americans say they feel isolated , and we’re getting together less and less
body: We are in the midst of a loneliness epidemic: More than half of Americans say they feel isolated , and we’re getting together less and less

In 2023, only about 4 percent of adults said they went to a party on a weekend or holiday.  According to Imogen Willetts , a party historian and author of the book Up All Night: A History of Going Out , this moment is an outlier.  “For most of human history, the experiences that we associate with nightlife — drinking, dancing, music, hedonism — those experiences were simply part of religion because religion was so all-encompassing,” she told Vox

If parties are so ingrained in humankind, then, what are we missing when we don’t get out the door on a Friday night anymore? And what lessons can we learn from the turnups of yore? We get into all of that and more — including how to throw a great party and how to be a good guest — on the latest episode Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Willetts, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545

Can you talk about the role religion played in early nightlife? Because I think we often think of religion and partying as two separate things, but that was not the case for all of history, was it? [Religion] contained people’s hedonistic instinct

And so there’s even evidence, which I love thinking about this, that the churchgoing experience in medieval England was actually quite rowdy and quite raucous.  On feast days there would be drinking, there would be dancing
And there’s one theory that wooden pews were introduced in Wells Cathedral in England to subdue the dancing because it was so raucous
And so in some sense, it takes us a while to get to nightlife because we sort of didn’t need it for a very long time
Religion contained hedonism quite comfortably within it

Seventeenth-century Japan, I would say, is the beginning of modern nightlife because we have these commercial party scenes, nightlife environments, which have nothing to do with religion,  “Whether it’s at a sports match or a concert stadium, and even within religion — that is collective effervescence.” Crucially, they’re also separate from court
Another part of party scenes is court spectacle — think Louis XIV and Versailles and all of that stuff that was contained within these monarchical structures
So the first real nightlife destination is Yoshiwara, which was built on the outskirts of Edo, which is now Tokyo
The idea of church being a place to party is so interesting
I do get the same feeling I get at church when I’m on the dance floor and I hear Kaytranada
I can imagine how these religious experiences allowed people to access that feeling of release through music and through dance

An expression that I came across when researching the book that I think really wonderfully kind of captures the essence of nightlife and partying is this term coined by the sociologist Émile Durkheim in 1912, which is “collective effervescence.” That’s the feeling that we experience during peak communal experiences.  Whether it’s at a sports match or a concert stadium, and even within religion — that is collective effervescence
That is the same sensation, that surge of euphoria that people feel on dance floors

I think parties and nightlife are such an important way to access this very important human feeling, particularly in societies that are increasingly atheist or increasingly secular.  We need nightlife to have these communal euphoric experiences and feel part of something bigger than ourselves
You’ve written about how, yes, parties are fun, but they’re also at the epicenter of some pretty important cultural and societal shifts
I think nightlife is very uniquely poised to allow for experimentation and innovation and transgression

Also, in a very practical way, if you’re part of the abstract expressionist scene of mid-century New York or something, you need somewhere to meet and talk to people and figure out how you’re going to sell your work that’s like nothing people have ever seen before.  These social spaces play a really, really important role in culture
The abstract expressionist artists were hanging out in the Cedar Tavern, and then you have things like the Viennese Secession Movement and Cabaret Fledermaus was part of that meeting space
Similarly, you get things like dance and music that’s very much created for dance floors, for clubbing, for nightlife: the can-can and then disco and then techno
Nightlife has been so crucial to the propulsion of culture

A lot of this is happening in the club, but what about parties happening in private homes ? One of the great examples of people opening up their homes in a sense of turning the home into a club was turn-of-the-century New Orleans
On Saturday nights, people would host fish fries: Basically, when you would open up your home to the public, you would charge entry at the door
Once inside, people were treated to this amazing spread of food, drink, and there would be bands that would perform
It was often a way for households who were struggling with rent payments to earn some extra cash
Langston Hughes writes about the Saturday night rent parties , where people’s apartments would be opened up in the exact same way
He said they were more interesting than anything that was going on in the cabarets and the clubs

He was going to those as often as he could and collecting the invitations for them.  People would write their address on business cards, leave them in different shops and pubs and hairdressers or whatever, and then you would pick them up and then go to the party
Langston Hughes collected them, and they now are randomly in a Yale archive of all places

As you think of parties over the centuries, are there elements that all the best parties have in common?  At their very core essence, you need good music, you need good lighting, and I think also you need to create this atmosphere where the sense that anything can happen

What you want is for the people that are at your party to feel like they can behave differently or do something a little bit wild.  I think that there’s something very satisfying in experiencing a domestic world upturned
I think seeing the kitchen become a gloomy cocktail bar, the living room becoming a dance floor — there’s something very satisfying in experiencing that
It goes back to what the heart of nightlife culture or party culture is all about
You want that sense of slight disorder that makes people feel alive.

title: Why Trump’s Latino voters are fleeing him
excerpt: Early voting signs on the doors of the Miami Beach North Shore Branch Public Library in Miami Beach, Florida, on December 7, 2025. | Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal
body: Early voting signs on the doors of the Miami Beach North Shore Branch Public Library in Miami Beach, Florida, on December 7, 2025. | Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images In 2024, Donald Trump’s victory was powered in large part by massive gains with Latino voters
He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016
But now, that support is plummeting; Trump’s approval rating among Latinos who voted for him recently fell from 93 percent to 66 percent , where it was at the beginning of his second term
Why? It has a lot to do, as with everything these days, with the economy.  It was the same in 2024
During that election, voters were experiencing rising costs and stagnant wages — the same trend that has continued until today
In 2024, though, Joe Biden and his administration — which also meant Vice President Kamala Harris — took the blame from all voters, and particularly Latinos

Today, the blame is falling on Trump.  America, Actually host Astead Herndon caught up with Stephanie Valencia, who co-founded Equis Research, a political research firm that specializes in Latino voters, to unpack some of these recent shifts and explain them.  “I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup,” she said on the podcast. “And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.” That’s why, when the economy is bad, this group is primed to be a “swinging giant” in US politics, Valencia explains — and right now, it appears to be swinging hard against Trump.  Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Equis has called Latinos one of the last great wild cards in American politics
Is that because of some of the double-digit swings that we’ve seen among this voting group over the past few elections? Yes, it absolutely has to do with that
Latinos often get given the title the “sleeping giant,” which I just want to get rid of from everybody’s vocabulary
We should be called the “swinging giant” based on how much shift we have seen election to election
A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical, and that swinging middle really is deciding every single election
Your playbook gets into messengers and particularly how we reach folks where they are

It makes a Spanish-Spanglish distinction talking about the different types of media that Latino voters consume.  I wanted to ask, in that vein, what’s the single biggest mistake campaigns make in terms of not reaching folks where they are? Oh man, how long do we have so I can tell you how many mistakes? They’re really simple unforced errors
I’m going to give a very concrete and simple example that I think illustrates that.  Look, I’m Latina
I grew up speaking mostly English, but I listen to Spanish-language radio
I watch a lot of YouTube, and on YouTube I’m watching people like Karol G and Carin León
A lot of people — a lot of Latino swing voters — have the same media consumption habits that I do
The first problem or challenge that a lot of candidates make is they just simply translate their English ad into Spanish
And that is, to me, one of the biggest mistakes because there are a lot of things that people want to be communicating in Spanish that don’t translate word for word
There are sayings in Spanish that don’t translate directly from English or more direct ways you can communicate
I’m sure it immediately reads Google Translate rather than an original message for said community
Mistake No. 2 is when they’re deploying that ad digitally, as a proxy for talking to people, they’re going to use Spanish-language browser settings

So they say, “We don’t want people who speak English to see the Spanish-language ad.” So the way they find that set of voters is just by going to people who have Spanish-language browser settings.  Like I said, I don’t have a Spanish-language browser setting
Everything I consume online is set in English on Chrome, but I still watch a lot of content in Spanish on YouTube

So you’re missing a voter like me who’s going to see a Spanish language ad from a James Talarico or a Manny Rutinel and be turned on by it because I’m going to say, “Hey, that candidate’s speaking to our community

That candidate has enough respect to develop a Spanish-language ad.”  We did some testing a couple of years ago that showed that over 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish think that party or candidate cares more about Latinos
Your research found that Project 2025 and Trump’s mass deportation plans were not top of mind for most people, and that they were thinking about the economy

I wanted to ask about that because I remember the RNC signs at the convention saying, “Mass deportations now.” One number says that 62 percent of Latinos now think that Trump wants to deport undocumented immigrants broadly.  Why did it take till post-election to realize those threats of mass deportation were real considering they were so front and center during his campaign? I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand the kind of news that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, is consuming

What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on people or Trump surrogates who said he was going to focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals
Fast-forward to 2026; the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration

They feel like there was a broken promise there.  They were told he was going to focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was going to focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that
And then add that to the litany of broken promises

I’m hearing a distinction between a focus on the border, which Republicans did try to prioritize rather than the interior deportations that may have been more attributed to Stephen Miller than Donald Trump
But we have certainly seen that be a focus of the administration once they came back into office
You mentioned the shift that has happened since 2024, and that’s really important, of course

Trump’s approval rating with Latinos is now worse than with non-Latinos, a stunning reversal in 18 months.  You mentioned the factors that have contributed there, but is this really just the economy? It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration

It’s those three things.  One thing that is really interesting to note about Trump’s approval, other than that it’s at basement levels — and he’s very much pulled down the GOP with him broadly and with Latino voters — is that in Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval on his total job
And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy

title: The scariest AI doom scenario you haven’t thought about
excerpt: At least, this is what a growing number of technologists and policymakers fear.  Last week, a lead researcher at Anthropic declared that there was a greate
body: At least, this is what a growing number of technologists and policymakers fear.  Last week, a lead researcher at Anthropic declared that there was a greater than 10 percent chance of AI “killing all humans” within the next decade

This nerve-racking forecast, combined with recent AI-initiated cyberattacks , have fueled calls for slowing the progress of artificial intelligence — a proposal that Anthropic and OpenAI subsequently embraced
Not all prophets of AI doom agree about precisely how this apocalypse would come about

Many focus on scenarios reminiscent of The Terminator films, in which superintelligent machines conspire to exterminate humanity — perhaps in the same not-quite-intentional way that humans laid waste to the dodo, or passenger pigeon
Key takeaways Synthetic pandemics are among the biggest existential risks facing humanity
AI could make bioweapons more powerful and easier to build
Governments can make us safer from both natural and artificial pathogens by investing more into pandemic preparedness

But there is another, arguably more intuitive way that AI could bring about mass death, if not human extinction: by making it easier for people to develop and deploy catastrophic bioweapons.  Importantly, this hypothetical doesn’t require AI models to become conscious or superintelligent; it merely requires them to accelerate preexisting trends in biotechnology.  For those alarmed by this hypothetical, the threat AI poses is essentially twofold

First, when combined with technological progress in gene editing and DNA synthesis, chatbots could vastly increase the number of people capable of assembling dangerous viruses already known to medical science
And the more potential bioengineers there are in the world, the higher the odds that one will prove to be a diligent psychopath

Second, AI could help highly trained biologists to discover — or engineer — a custom supervirus, which could then fall into the wrong hands.  Recent headlines have lent some credence to both of these fears.  Earlier this year, biologists warned that, with a few simple prompts, they’d gotten chatbots to dispense detailed instructions for engineering a treatment-resistant strain of an infamous pathogen, step-by-step protocols for recreating a once-pandemic virus, and advice on dispersing biological payloads via weather balloon
In August, a team of scientists revealed that an AI model trained on DNA sequences had generated blueprints for deadly viruses unseen in nature (albeit, viruses deadly to bacteria , not animals)
And last week, Anthropic announced that it had thwarted several suspected attempts by state actors to use Claude for bioweapons research
Precisely how much AI is increasing the risk of an artificial pandemic is unclear
Even before ChatGPT, advances in synthetic biology were already making bioengineering tools more potent and accessible
And even after four years of rapid AI progress, the technical barriers to engineering novel superviruses remain formidable
Regardless, there is a great deal more that governments can — and should — be doing to protect us from synthetic pandemics, both manmade and natural
No matter what AI’s ultimate impact on biosecurity proves to be, now is the time to both prepare for the worst-case scenario and, ideally, preempt it

Why synthetic superviruses are scary Before we dig into how AI could raise the risk of a man-made pandemic, it’s worth spelling out why that prospect is so unnerving.  Put simply, few things could more credibly destroy civilization — and/or, the human species — than a synthetic supervirus
Infectious diseases have killed more humans than any other force on Earth
The Black Death wiped out at least 30 percent of all Europeans in the 1300s , while the 1918 flu killed 50 million people worldwide

You don’t need me to tell you what things were like in 2020 (or how much worse they could have been, if vaccines hadn’t been rolled out in record time).  And nature kicked off these catastrophes without even trying
A bioterrorist consciously seeking to maximize human death could theoretically improve on evolution’s handiwork

If biotech continues to advance — and scientists identify viral genomes that reliably yield high transmissibility and lethality — a malicious actor might one day be able to manufacture a virus that’s both as contagious as measles and as deadly as Ebola.  Natural selection generally disfavors viruses that are both highly transmissible and profoundly fatal; bugs that kill their hosts too reliably often have difficulty spreading
Yet a virus with a long asymptomatic period could escape this tradeoff
For example, HIV can live in a person’s body for a decade before generating noticeable symptoms
In theory, a highly contagious respiratory virus could similarly lie in wait for many weeks, months, or even years
If bioterrorists ever managed to unleash an easily transmitted, highly fatal virus, they could shake the foundations of modern existence
In that scenario, reliably showing up for work might require accepting a 50-50 chance  of getting yourself — and your family — brutally killed

Covid never required essential workers to assume risks anywhere near this high (the virus had a less than 1 percent case fatality rate among prime-age workers, before vaccines became available). Although there are many heroes among us, plenty of doctors, nurses, warehouse workers, power plant technicians, delivery drivers, and other essential laborers might not tolerate a coin flip’s chance of wiping out their loved ones
And if enough sheltered in place, systems for producing and distributing healthcare, food, water, and power could swiftly break down

Humanity’s “Joker” problem All this invites the question: Who would ever want to do this?  After all, viruses are terrible weapons: They’re difficult to make, impossible to control, and jeopardize the lives of those who cultivate and distribute them
Partly for these reasons, biological weapons have hardly ever been used ; the last fatal bioterror attacks were the anthrax mailings of 2001

To this, anxious biosecurity experts might reply, to quote the former British intelligence officer Alfred Pennyworth : “Some men just want to watch the world burn.” Mass shooters regularly forfeit their lives to the cause of killing others at random
And brilliant iconoclasts periodically develop murderous ideologies; Ted Kaczynski, the Harvard mathematician turned Unabomber, wished to bring about the collapse of industrial civilization
And every once in a while, an aspiring supervillain gets graduate training in virology
In the 1990s, the Kyoto University-educated genetic engineer Seiichi Endo joined Japan’s Aum Shinrikyo death cult
Drawing on the group’s $1 billion in funds , Endo sought to weaponize Ebola , Q fever , botulinum, and anthrax — with the aim of killing as many nonbelievers as possible.  Of course, Endo failed

And lone wolf psychopaths have never gotten their hands on anything more lethal than an assault weapon, bomb, or airplane.  But some scientists believe that technological advances — including generative AI — may provide the Endos and Kaczynskis of tomorrow with catastrophic power.  How AI and biotech could democratize bioterrorism MIT biologist Kevin Esvelt is among his field’s most prominent Cassandras

title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
excerpt: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Eq
body: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison
About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US

Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next

title: Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died
excerpt: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children Survivors from a prison cell
body: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna

The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger

title: The Download: AI’s extinction risk and bioweapons threat
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Could AI really kill us all? Your questions, answered On Wednesday, MIT Technology Review hosted a live Roundtables event that asked the question many seem to be asking right now: could AI really kill us all? But attendees had more questions than we had time to answer, so we asked senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins to tackle some of the best ones.  The questions they tried to answer include: am I going to die? Why should AI kill us, if at all? Is AI really dangerous, or is it just tech companies drumming up PR? And what steps can be taken to make sure AI is controlled, monitored and regulated effectively?
